item.description: arXiv:2607.27042v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Adaptive rounding methods such as GPTQ quantize the weights of a large language model (LLM) one at a time, propagating each rounding error to the weights not yet rounded. YAQA lowers the KL divergence from the original model with two-sided adaptive rounding under a Kronecker-factored Hessian, but its error feedback takes quartic work in the size of a square layer. We present GPTQ-2D, which provably computes the same rounding with cubic work, while still rounding the entries of each anti-diagonal in parallel. Its GPU implementation uses two levels of blocking to improve hardware utilization. We also extend the algorithm to Hessians with any number of Kronecker factors. In our experiments, GPTQ-2D is as accurate as YAQA and cuts the time to quantize Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU from 8.6 days to 1.6 hours. Source code is available at https://github.com/IST-DASLab/GPTQ-2D.

item.title: Twig: Parallel and Memory-Efficient Tree Speculative Decoding for Hybrid-Attention LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2608.01651v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Emerging LLMs increasingly interleave full attention with recurrent linear attention to reduce long-context serving costs. Tree speculative decoding could further accelerate these hybrid models, but recurrent linear-attention layers carry parent-dependent states. Existing engines therefore verify proposal trees sequentially and snapshot the full state per node, causing latency and memory to grow with tree and batch sizes. We present Twig, a kernel--runtime co-design for tree speculative decoding of hybrid LLMs. Twig derives a tree-structured factorization of the linear-attention recurrence and realizes it with a resource-efficient GPU kernel that verifies all nodes in parallel, accelerating linear-attention tree verification by 3.4--7.7$\times$. It losslessly represents speculative state updates as token-level factors and reconstructs only the accepted state, reducing transient state memory by 82--99$\times$ and freeing GPU memory for KV caches. We integrate Twig into SGLang, a widely deployed production LLM serving engine, and further optimize its runtime through batch-wide verification budgeting. Across four models, two GPU platforms, and diverse datasets, Twig achieves up to $4.72\times$ the offline decode throughput of autoregressive decoding and up to $2.03\times$ that of the strongest tree-speculative baseline. Under online agent workloads, Twig reduces TTFT and TPOT by up to $67.6\%$ and $49.9\%$, respectively, over the strongest tree-speculative baseline.

item.title: Effective pruning of task-trained recurrent neural networks using noisy fluctuations and connection rescaling
item.description: arXiv:2608.05464v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pruning network connections is key to brain function but, despite its importance, there exist few biologically-plausible pruning rules with demonstrated good performance. We evaluate noise-prune, a recently introduced unsupervised local pruning rule for recurrent networks that uses noisy fluctuations to determine the importance of connections. Noise-prune has previously only been empirically tested on random networks without a specific computational function. We show that noise-prune preserves task-performance in task-trained recurrent neural networks, greatly outperforming a strategy that only uses connection magnitude and exceeding a non-local strategy that uses second-order information. Rather than deterministically removing connections that fall below a threshold, noise-prune samples connections to preserve based on their importance and strengthens retained connections to preserve average strength. We show that this sampling and rescaling is essential to good performance, and can augment other pruning strategies. We also find that the optimal empirical degree of rescaling is lower than predicted by the original theoretical argument, and thus develop a new version of noise-prune that outperforms the previous version. Our results demonstrate that a biologically-motivated pruning strategy based on local activity statistics can effectively preserve task performance in functional recurrent networks by combining activity-dependent connection selection with compensatory strengthening of surviving connections.

item.title: Inference and Uncertainty Quantification for Streaming $r$-PCA
item.description: arXiv:2608.18374v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We address two open questions in streaming PCA via Oja's algorithm: sharp operator-norm convergence for general rank under sub-Gaussian data, and distributional inference for the resulting subspace estimator. Existing convergence analyses, even in the rank-one case, either assume bounded data or leave non-vanishing remainder terms that prevent adaptation to a polynomially vanishing tail spectrum, while existing distributional results are confined to the rank-one case. Our convergence theory removes these remainder terms and yields a sharp rate. In the dense-tail spiked covariance regime, this rate matches the minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. More generally, we prove a matching lower bound, up to logarithmic factors, across both dense-tail and sparse-tail regimes under a mild nondegeneracy condition. The analysis yields a linearization of Oja's iterates, which in turn enables a high-dimensional Gaussian approximation for the general-rank subspace estimation error with an explicit limiting covariance. We also establish a row-wise Gaussian approximation over convex sets for the aligned difference, recovering prior rank-one results as special cases. For practical inference, we develop an online multiplier bootstrap algorithm and prove its consistency. Beyond streaming PCA, our techniques contribute to Gaussian approximation and bootstrap inference for nonconvex stochastic approximation.

item.title: Speed limits for information acquisition in stochastic learning dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2609.08219v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural networks acquire internal representations through learning. In this work, we formulate stochastic gradient descent (SGD) as a Markovian stochastic process and derive a Fisher-information flow speed limit that bounds the rate at which trainable parameters can acquire information about data-generating parameters. The resulting inequality decomposes the upper bound on the information flow into drift and noise contributions, thereby quantifying the roles of deterministic learning forces and SGD-induced fluctuations from an information-theoretic perspective. We verify the bound in analytically tractable basis-function linear regression, where the information budget predicted by the bound reproduces the ordering and characteristic time scales with which different data-generating parameters are encoded in the learned parameters. These results establish Fisher-information speed limits as a quantitative framework for understanding which properties of the data-generating process are acquired, in what order, and how rapidly they can be encoded in the trainable parameters.

item.title: Counterexamples and Sufficient Conditions: Comments on "Optimally-Transported Generalized Method of Moments"
item.description: arXiv:2609.20260v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We comment on the optimally-transported generalized method of moments (OTGMM) of Schennach and Starck (2026) and give counterexamples to Theorems 2-6. In the small-error analysis, the assumptions do not ensure consistency or asymptotic normality (Theorems 2-3). In the large-error analysis, Theorem 4 states the equivalence between the OTGMM estimator and the GMM estimator with modified moments, and Theorems 5-6 assert consistency and asymptotic normality. Through counterexamples, we show that the equivalence in Theorem 4 fails and a component of the Lagrange multiplier has different limits under the two estimators (Theorems 5-6). We also point out that, under misspecification, the population value selected by OTGMM depends on the metric. We give sufficient conditions and establish results following the original motivation for OTGMM. Our corrections to Theorems 4-6 change their assumptions or interpretation more substantially than those to Theorems 2 and 3. Furthermore, we correct Assumption 16 and the test's null distribution.

item.title: PROSWIN: Probabilistic Solar Wind Speed Forecasting Using Deep Distributional Regression From Solar Images
item.description: arXiv:2609.26683v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurately predicting fast solar wind conditions is challenging, as uncertainties are large and unquantified by traditional single-value prediction models. In particular, the risks of high-speed solar wind streams (HSSs), which can cause damage to technological infrastructure, cannot be reliably assessed without probabilistic forecasts. We present PROSWIN, a probabilistic machine learning model that forecasts the hourly solar wind speed (SWS) at Earth with a four-day lead time. The approach combines solar images and magnetograms using a deep neural network coupled to a distributional regression algorithm. Because standard error metrics underweight the relevance of HSS peaks, we further introduce the prediction score, a model-selection metric that jointly rewards timeline and HSS peak accuracy. On 14 years of data, our forecast achieves very well-calibrated uncertainties (<1% average deviation). Using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), a metric that assesses distributional accuracy, we obtain a timeline CRPS of 41.0 km/s, an HSS peak CRPS of 45.3 km/s, and a prediction score of 42.3 km/s. We find that the 171 {\AA} channel is an important complement to the typically used 193 {\AA} and 211 {\AA} channels and that the prediction score for model selection improves the applicability of the model. Compared to selected models from the literature, ours is the only one that is accurate for both timeline and HSS peak values, rather than trading one off against the other. These results support the advantages of probabilistic over single-value solar wind models. The introduced methods are also transferable to other forecasting problems.

item.title: Undertone: Personalizing Frozen VLM Aesthetic Judges from Few Ratings
item.description: arXiv:2609.27110v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Image quality assessment predicts a mean opinion score (MOS), but for image aesthetics the mean hides the individual, so personalized assessment must start from the few images a new user rates. Fitting each person from scratch fails with ten ratings; networks fine-tuned per person carry over poorly to new kinds of images. We present Undertone-P, which learns from other raters a Gaussian prior over per-person regression weights on read-outs of frozen vision-language model (VLM) judges: the probability-weighted rating and the hidden state at the score token. Since people differ from the crowd in ways other raters reveal, a few ratings need only choose among those ways: a new user costs one closed-form solve, and no network is trained. On Ryu and Yanaka's PARA benchmark, the prior alone reaches a Spearman correlation of .640, above the best published 10- and 100-rating results (.581 and .620); 10 and 100 of a person's ratings raise it to .648 and .676. These ratings add most where tastes depart from the crowd: with 100 ratings, +.067 for the raters who agree least with it and +.206 on LAPIS artworks, against +.037 overall. Without labels, the judges' expected scores predict PARA's MOS at .835 (best published model we ran: .694). PARA-trained networks still lead under PARA's original protocol, likely through a stronger end-to-end MOS model.

item.title: Structural and Representational Agency in LLM-Driven Timbre Generation and Interpolation
item.description: arXiv:2610.12532v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative creative interfaces routinely report the user's position within a space of possibilities. Such displays imply that the quantities shown were measured from the artefact; in a growing class of systems they are instead predicted by a language model describing its own output, and the two are indistinguishable on screen. Most creative domains lack an agreed measurement against which such a self-report can be checked; audio admits one. In a measurement study of a working LLM-driven timbre interface, what a user can cause proves separable from what the interface reports. The first is exactly characterisable: the reachable set is a zonotope in parameter space whose dimension increases by one per sound placed, so the space the model may act within is demonstrably the user's own. The second is inaccurate. The displayed position differs from measurement by approximately three times the width of that region, and the error has two independent sources: model-predicted coordinates, whose accuracy varies twofold between the two models evaluated, and the interpolation step, which arises from combining synthesiser parameters and is unaffected by model quality. End to end, 27 of 36 refinement instructions produced no perceptible change, and under the weaker model the facility performed no action while reporting convergence. Effective agency (what a user can cause) and epistemic agency (whether they can know it) are therefore separable and independently engineered: structurally enforced constraints survive model failure, whereas guarantees resting on the model's own report do not. The failure mode that remains is silence presented as success. We close with a short protocol for building and auditing such displays.

item.title: Single-stage joint diffusion of sky images and clear-sky index for ultra-short-term irradiance forecasting: what the frame-to-irradiance stage discards
item.description: arXiv:2610.21795v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sky-image irradiance forecasting is dominated by a two-stage design: a video-prediction model forecasts future sky frames, and a separately trained regressor maps those frames to irradiance. We propose a single-stage alternative that co-denoises the future sky-image and clear-sky-index sequences in one diffusion process, with an irradiance head that reads a denoised preview of the future sky rather than the noised diffusion state. The forecaster needs no regression stage and runs from sky images and deterministic covariates alone, with no measured irradiance at its input --- the situation at a site with a camera but no pyranometer. On 2023 SIRTA data the model reaches a pooled RMSE of $104.1$~W\,m$^{-2}$ and a skill score of $+0.34$ on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) against smart persistence, higher than any of twelve baseline configurations, and retains that skill when retrained on 2021--2022. On the model's own generated frames, a separately trained regressor reaches $150.6$~W\,m$^{-2}$ against the joint head's $104.1$: roughly $46$~W\,m$^{-2}$ that joint training recovers and a cascade discards. Point accuracy is competitive but not best: a deterministic network that also reads measured irradiance attains $97.6$~W\,m$^{-2}$. The model's CRPS skill leads that network's in every sky-condition tertile, by $0.26$ to $0.30$.

item.title: No Escape from the Quadratic Barrier: Adaptive Attacks on Linear $\ell_2$ Sketches
item.description: arXiv:2610.25008v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Linear sketches estimate properties of high-dimensional inputs from a fixed low-dimensional projection. At constant accuracy, randomized Euclidean-norm sketches, notably the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform, support exponentially many nonadaptive queries in sketch dimension $k$. For adaptive black-box queries, known privacy-based defenses guarantee $\widetilde{\Omega}(k^2)$ and it remained open whether stronger guarantees were possible. Prior attacks used more queries, restricted the responder, or provided weaker failure guarantees. We show that the quadratic guarantee is optimal up to logarithmic factors, even with a computationally unbounded responder that knows the matrix, attack algorithm, history, and query distributions and may change its randomized rule after every query. For every fixed hidden $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}$ with $n>40k$ and target accuracy $\alpha \in (0,1]$, our black-box attack uses $O(k+\alpha^2k^2\log(2+\alpha^2k))$ queries in $\widetilde{O}(1+\alpha^2k)$ adaptive rounds to force, with constant probability, a round in which a constant fraction of answers have $\Omega(\alpha)$ relative error. This fraction can be taken arbitrarily close to one half. Our results clarify the limits of defending a fixed compressive linear representation by adapting the prediction rule.

item.title: Memory before Goal: Role of Pre-History Memory for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.31166v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation in dynamic scenes is non-Markovian: cues vanish as objects change or are hidden, or leave the view as the robot turns and walks, yet whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies see only the present. We present WholeBodyMem, an object-guided perceptual memory that keeps the pre-history of object events seen before the robot acts on its goal. SAM3 tracks the task objects, and their events causally select key frames within an adaptive budget, which the action expert reads by cross-attention together with object tokens encoding appearance, geometry and time. We also contribute HuMeGo, a humanoid memory benchmark with six simulated and six real-world Unitree G1 tasks. Keeping the right frames rather than more frames, WholeBodyMem surpasses memoryless and uniform-memory baselines, raising its base policy's success from 29.1% to 72.6% in simulation and from 36.7% to 88.3% on the real robot, while also improving the standard SIMPLE tasks (70.2% to 86.9%).

item.title: Global $\mathcal{O}\left(k^{-2}\right)$ Convergence of Multilevel Gradient-Regularized Newton Methods
item.description: arXiv:2610.35195v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop and analyze multilevel gradient-regularized Newton methods for unconstrained convex optimization with Lipschitz-continuous Hessians. By computing Newton corrections in lower-dimensional subspaces, the proposed methods aim to reduce computational costs while preserving the global $\mathcal{O}\left(k^{-2}\right)$ convergence rate in function values of the full-space method. To establish this rate for multilevel methods, we introduce a class of row-nested restriction operators that ensures monotonicity of the reduced-gradient norms across levels. Numerical experiments with row-nested operators demonstrate convergence behavior comparable to full-space gradient-regularized Newton, while offering substantial computational savings on large-scale instances.

item.title: Sampling Design and Confidence Tubes for Integral Curves on Riemannian Manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2611.00771v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We estimate the integral curve of an unknown vector field from noisy tangent vector field on a known compact Riemannian manifold. We consider two sampling settings: independent observations at random locations that have already been collected, and a fixed response budget that allows subsequent locations to be chosen using pilot information. Under suitable regularity assumptions, the passive kernel estimator has curve error of order $n^{-2/(d+3)}$ in probability, with sample size $n$ and manifold dimension $d$. Its functional central limit theorem has a limit characterized by a linear stochastic differential equation. For active sampling, an independent pilot directs one new batch of measurements to neighborhoods of the target curve. Under localization, smoothness and design conditions, this concentration yields expected maximum curve error of order $N^{-1/2}$, including the pilot in the total response budget $N$. Both methods provide simultaneous geodesic confidence tubes with asymptotically exact coverage under mild conditions. Simulations show narrower active tubes in most reported settings, with improved small-sample coverage in some three-dimensional examples. Ocean-drifter observations illustrate mean-flow reconstruction on the sphere, and a canopy-flow LDA application uses retrospective active sampling to quantify lateral and vertical departures of local mean streamlines.

item.title: Write Facts the Way Models Read Them: Lifting the Two-Hop Curse
item.description: arXiv:2611.01519v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A language model that learns a new fact by fine-tuning can repeat it but cannot reason with it: taught that a person is a citizen of a new country, it still cannot say, without chain-of-thought, who the head of state of that person's country is. This two-hop curse is widely treated as a reasoning deficit, and the strongest knowledge editors answer it with synthesized reasoning data. We show that the reasoning is intact and the writing is wrong. Fine-tuning writes a new fact as an answer to be said, whereas the second hop reads the bridge ("that person's country") as an entity, from the middle layers on: patching the model's own representation of the entity into the bridge at those layers largely restores the second hop, yet after fine-tuning the bridge there is no closer to the new entity than before the edit. We therefore propose read-equivalent writing (Legible): one loss term makes the bridge phrase, at the layer where the second hop finishes reading it, match the model's own reading of the new entity, and keeps the same relation's other subjects unchanged. Phrases and targets come from the edited model itself, and no multi-hop training data is used. Across Qwen2.5, Llama-3 and Qwen3, Legible (I) composes learned facts more often than the model composes its own knowledge, on MQuAKE's two-hop-curse questions; (II) reaches 1.8-2.6x the bridge accuracy of CaKE, whose reasoning data composes no better than plain fine-tuning, and has the best average over composition, accuracy and locality against four families of writers; and (III) lifts the curse on RippleEdits, on the benchmark of Balesni et al., who named the curse, and at 14B.

item.title: Seeing Why: Exact Evidence Maps for Quantum and Optical Image Classifiers
item.description: arXiv:2611.01993v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When an image classifier decides, we can usually only estimate why. For quantum and all-optical classifiers that act linearly on amplitude-encoded pictures up to the measurement, with no trained classical network before or after them, each class's Born probability above its no-information share, $P_g - b_g$, splits exactly into contributions of the encoded amplitudes, shown as Born evidence maps (BEM). The split itself follows from known results on quadratic forms: with the transmitted light held fixed, it is what Integrated Gradients from a zero baseline and the Shapley value give. What we add is a way to measure it on the hardware that classifies, from class probabilities on a quantum chip or, in simulation, from camera frames on a lens bench, with no gradient circuit and no light sent backwards; a $g\times g$ map takes $1 + 2g^2$ runs. Deleting the 5% of pixels with the highest evidence drops accuracy from 73% to 9% (one seed), as occlusion and gradient $\times$ input do, while plain gradients remove much less. The classifiers share one architecture, a Fourier-plane mask followed by a brickwall circuit on qubits or by phase plates on a lens bench, read by a fixed Born headroom readout with no trained parameter; centring each picture on its own mean lets dark features count as much as bright ones. In simulation, four phase plates at one wavelength reach 72.3% on Caltech-10 colour photographs. On IBM's ibm_kingston, with the mask computed classically before approximate loading, 300 test pictures were classified at 37.7% against 10% chance (56.3% in exact simulation), and $2\times2$ maps of the filtered input of 30 test pictures drawn at random in advance, measured on the chip, agreed with the exact ones ($r = 0.88$; standard estimator 0.82). The maps also revealed a shortcut in the data; as the trim that removed it was chosen on test pictures, the Caltech-10 results are exploratory.

item.title: Distinguishing Initial-Condition and Model Error Using Machine-Learning Weather Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.05592v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Differentiable weather models allow atmospheric initial conditions to be directly optimized to shadow a known trajectory, which we take from a reanalysis dataset. Here, we extend this optimization to include the forecast model, GraphCast, using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). We compare model optimization with initial-condition (IC) optimization, and then joint optimization, where both are tuned simultaneously. When compared against a control forecast initialized with reanalysis data, LoRA and IC optimization individually produce similar improvements. We find similar results when IC and LoRA are jointly optimized across a spectrum of solutions where a tuning coefficient smoothly shifts the weight of the joint optimization from all-LoRA to all-IC; forecast improvement is not unique to the relative contributions of model and IC corrections. To better discriminate the source of error, we introduce a second model, Pangu-Weather, as a supervisor that gates IC updates during joint optimization. This gated optimization is the same as before, except that IC updates at each epoch are accepted only when they improve the forecasts of both models; otherwise, only the LoRA update is accepted. Results show that this cross-model constraint substantially improves agreement between the two models in their response to the same optimized ICs, narrowing the gap in mean forecast error reduction from 64% to 10%. Moreover, when used together, the LoRA and IC corrections from the gated optimization yield GraphCast forecast improvements similar to those from the ungated optimization. These results imply that model error that is encoded in the ungated ICs is shifted to the LoRA corrections via gating, yielding IC corrections that may provide better analysis estimates.

item.title: ZipDrift: Generating Multimodal Short-Horizon MPC Costs with One-Step Drifting Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.05793v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Short-horizon model predictive control (MPC) is fast but myopic. ZipMPC compensates by learning a context-dependent correction of the short-horizon cost that imitates a long-horizon expert. We observe that the optimal correction is often multimodal: when a slower opponent can be passed on either side, good corrections of opposite sign coexist, and the expert's choice between them hinges on tiny cost differences. Deterministic regression then averages modes or inherits inconsistent expert tie-breaking. We propose ZipDrift, which trains a one-step drifting generator over MPC cost corrections, tilted toward low closed-loop cost and learned only from cost evaluations of candidate corrections, without differentiating through the optimiser. A few generated candidates are ranked by a learned critic, and the model-based MPC then enforces dynamics and constraints. In a kinematic overtaking benchmark derived from ZipMPC, more than half of the contexts are bimodal and the manual short-horizon MPC crashes in 28% of them. With an eight-dimensional stagewise correction, evaluated on 1000 fresh contexts and five training seeds, ZipDrift with eight candidates crashes in 0.74% of episodes, compared with 3.4% for an idealised ZipMPC-style regressor and 2.1% for critic-ranked random candidates with the same budget. A mixture density network (MDN) with the same selection is equally good (0.76%). The benefit of drifting lies in sample quality: in a pre-specified test on further unseen contexts, a single drifting sample crashes in 8.7% of episodes against 13.2% for the MDN, and ZipDrift needs four candidates instead of eight to fall below 1%. With many candidates, all methods degrade as selection exploits errors of the critic.

item.title: Contextual Pictograms for Repairing Multilingual ASR Errors
item.description: arXiv:2611.05637v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech transcription errors can be difficult to recognize when competing word hypotheses are unfamiliar or visually similar. We describe an interface that combines alternative transcripts, replay and contextually checked pictograms for selected uncertain concepts. The system will initially support French and Spanish functional utterances. A counterbalanced study will assess whether pictorial feedback helps listeners recover the speaker's intended action beyond text alternatives alone. We will also quantify semantic mismatch and additional interaction time, since an inappropriate image can reinforce the wrong interpretation rather than repair it.

item.title: The Male Abstraction Bias in Internet Culture and Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.05730v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conceptual abstraction and gender are two equally central aspects of the human mind, yet they have traditionally been studied in isolation from one another, as though they were fundamentally separate. Here, we find gender and abstraction are systematically linked throughout the space of concepts spanning single (N = 40,000) and multi-word expressions (N = 67,000): across billions of words and millions of images on the internet --- and across numerous measurement techniques, including human and AI classifications --- more abstract concepts are more associated with men, a pattern we show replicates in languages around the world. This male abstraction bias not only holds across semantic domains, but it also maps onto grammatical structure: verbs and adverbs are more abstract and more male-coded, revealing a system-wide trace of stereotypes accentuating agentic qualities in men. Furthermore, we show this bias readily emerges in the free associations humans and AIs produce in controlled online tasks, indicating its psychological internalization and its algorithmic reproduction. These findings identify a latent structure in conceptual space that unifies a range of stereotypes: for example, framings of women as more embodied, emotional, and warm, versus men as more cognitive, rational, and competent; as well as erroneous views of men as better at mathematics, science, and engineering. More broadly, by analyzing an unprecedentedly large, multimodal sample of online data, we provide culture-wide evidence of gender as a core organizing principle shaping conceptual space far beyond the characterization of people and social roles.

item.title: Logically Augmented Quantum LDPC Codes: Construction and Hierarchical Decoding
item.description: arXiv:2611.07062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a joint framework for constructing and decoding Logically Augmented (LA) quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. This is motivated by the need for flexible coding rates and adaptive error protection while preserving block length and code structure. On the construction side, we use an auxiliary \textit{Logical Protection Code (LPC)} to impose additional stabilizer constraints on selected logical qubits of a \textit{primary} code. On the decoding side, the proposed decoder uses the LPC syndrome to generate logical error hypotheses and condition belief propagation (BP) on each hypothesis. The proposed \textit{Hierarchical Logical List Decoder (HLLD)} is invoked only when the initial BP decoder for primary code fails to converge. It then selects the correction with the smallest Hamming weight among the syndrome-consistent candidates produced by hypothesis-conditioned BP runs. For numerical evaluation, we focus on short repetition LPCs, which provide a flexible means of trading rate for additional error protection. Each LPC syndrome admits exactly two logical error hypotheses, irrespective of repetition length, which enables HLLD to explore both possibilities without relying on a single logical estimate. Numerical results show that varying the repetition length provides a tunable trade-off between rate and error-correction performance across a wide range of primary code constructions and their operating regimes. On the decoding side, with the overall LA code held fixed, HLLD reduces the logical error rate by up to 81\%, 75\%, and 69\% for LA codes based on mitten, lifted-product, and bivariate bicycle codes, respectively, compared with conventional BP decoding of the same LA codes.

item.title: Elapsed-Service-Time-Aware Preemption for Age of Information Minimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.07151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the age of information and peak age of information in status update systems with an arbitrary number of independent sources sharing a single server with generally distributed service times. We consider a general age-dependent self-preemptive policy in which an in-service update from source $c$ is preempted by a new same-source arrival with a probability $p_c(x)$ that depends on the elapsed service time $x$. This formulation subsumes the non-preemptive, fully self-preemptive, and probabilistically preemptive policies as special cases, and also accommodates threshold-based preemption. We develop a unified analytical framework based on non-homogeneous absorbing continuous-time Markov chains and semi-Markov chains to derive explicit expressions for the average age of information and peak age of information of each source under general per-source service-time distributions and age-dependent preemption rules. The framework applies to both single-source and multi-source systems and enables joint tuning of per-source preemption parameters. Numerical results for fifteen service-time distributions in the single-source setting reveal that the benefits of preemption depend strongly on the service-time hazard-rate structure, with threshold-based preemption providing its most notable additional gains over age-independent policies for distributions with unimodal hazard rates. For a dual-source system with lognormal service times, jointly tuned threshold-based preemption achieves lower sum average age of information and peak age of information than the considered age-independent policies, highlighting the importance of cross-source interactions in preemption decisions.

item.title: Lossless Source Coding with Marginal Distribution Constraint
item.description: arXiv:2611.07156v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider lossless source coding with a marginal distribution constraint on the encoding symbols (SC-MDC). Unlike distribution matching, signal shaping and homophonic coding which require the symbols to be (approximately) i.i.d. following a target distribution, SC-MDC requires each symbol to have a marginal distribution that exactly matches the target distribution, which can be regarded as a perfect perceptual quality constraint on the symbols, and may have applications to wear leveling, source coding with cost and steganography. We give nonasymptotic lower and upper bounds on the optimal encoding length, and exactly characterize the coding rate (or the first-order term of the length) when the source distribution or the target distribution is uniform, or when the source is an i.i.d. sequence.

item.title: Functional Converses for Private Matrix-Product Retrieval under Library-Wide Decoder-Side Correlation
item.description: arXiv:2611.07325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider private retrieval of the matrix product $A^\top B^{(\theta)}$ from replicated $P_c$-colluding servers when $B^{(\ell)}=A+N^{(\ell)}$, with the innovations mutually independent and independent of the user-held $A\in\mathbb{F}_q^{m\times m}$. The servers store the full library, correlated with $A$, which changes both the communication problem and the security definition: a secrecy condition including the stored library cannot hold, as the library itself partly reveals $A$. We therefore measure only additional leakage and require index privacy conditioned on $A$; both reduce to classical notions under independence. For $A$ of rank $k<m$ we prove, with no structural hypothesis on the map, $D^*\geq H(A^\top B^{(\theta)}\mid A)/C_{\mathrm{PIR}}(N,P_c,L)-o(km)$, where $C_{\mathrm{PIR}}(N,P_c,L)$ is the replicated $P_c$-colluding private-information-retrieval capacity. The proof rests on a colluding converse for servers storing arbitrary refinements of the demanded messages, whose answers need not be measurable functions of the functional-message library, and a privacy-transfer characterization. Publishing a canonical row-space representative makes the bound achievable for arbitrary independent and identically distributed innovations under a public-setup measure. Under a strengthened observational model (exact correctness, common conditional library support, and full-transcript security), concealment forces $D\geq H(G_m N^{(\theta)})/C_{\mathrm{PIR}}$, where $G_m$ spans the linear join of all row spaces in the support of the operand distribution; this extends to vanishing error under a simultaneous-decodability assumption. In the full-rank case product recovery reduces to innovation recovery: $D^*=H(N^{(\theta)})/C_{\mathrm{PIR}}+o(m^2)$.

item.title: Energy-Time Optimal Decoding Using Expander-Graph LDPC Codes and Mesh Network Architecture
item.description: arXiv:2611.07336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Within the Thompson VLSI model, the first energy optimal decoding schemes (up to polylogarithmic factors) that also reach clock cycle lower bounds are constructed. Let $N$ be block length. Then, there is an exponential error scaling function and a binary symmetric channel, such that for all $f(N)$ that scales to zero more slowly than this, there is a decoding scheme for this channel with error probability that scales as $O(f(N))$ that has number of clock cycles $T\le O(\sqrt{-\log(f(N)})\text{polylog}(N))$ and energy $E\le O(N\sqrt{-\log(f(N))}\text{polylog}(N))$. This matches fundamental lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. The technique uses expander-graph based LDPC codes, a mesh network architecture, and a parallelization technique. The key technical result needed for this is a lemma in graph theory. This lemma is used to show that communication graphs of bounded node degree can be routed through two- and three-dimensional mesh networks without overflowing the memory of any mesh node. Upper bounds are also extended to three dimensions.

item.title: Combinatorial limitations of list-decoding Reed-Solomon codes
item.description: arXiv:2611.07607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For infinitely many rates $R \in (0,1)$, we show that full-length Reed-Solomon codes over fields of low characteristic can contain super-polynomially many codewords in a Hamming ball of radius just exceeding the Johnson radius. Over prime fields, we exhibit full-length Reed-Solomon codes of constant rate $R$ with polynomially many codewords in a Hamming ball of relative radius bounded strictly below $1-R$. This refutes a recent conjecture that, over prime fields, list sizes below capacity are always bounded by a constant. Together, these results demonstrate that certain restrictions in recent works on explicit Reed-Solomon codes achieving list-decoding capacity, related to the choice of field or evaluation points or to the list-size guarantee, are inherent.

item.title: A Universal Threshold Theory for Local Properties of Random Linear Codes
item.description: arXiv:2611.07661v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thresholds for local properties tell us which guarantees to expect from random linear codes (RLCs) and help us carry those guarantees over to structured codes. A monotone property is $b$-local if a collection of at most $b$ codewords can witness its satisfaction or failure, as in list decoding and list recovery. The threshold of $\mathcal P$ is the code dimension at which the probability that an RLC in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$ satisfies $\mathcal P$ crosses $1/2$ in a sharp transition. We show that the threshold of a $b$-local property $\mathcal P$ is within $O(b)$ dimensions of the expectation threshold. This is the dimension predicted by the best union bound over covers of $\mathcal P$: families of subspaces such that the span of every witness contains at least one member. This gives a general derandomization statement: Any decreasing local property satisfied by RLCs at a given rate holds at a similar rate for pseudorandom ensembles that fool the cover union bound. In addition to previously studied ensembles, these include codes whose parity-check matrix is sampled from a small-bias distribution. Because our threshold characterization applies to all local properties, this derandomization also reaches properties beyond the scope of earlier reductions, including maximum loads in linear hashing for arbitrary input sets, rank-metric list decoding, and list decoding from insertion-deletion errors and burst errors. Our theorem unifies and strengthens prior works on row-symmetric and coordinate-wise linear characterizations, which located the threshold to within $O(q^{2b}\log_q n)$ and $O(b^2+nb/\log_2 q)$ dimensions, respectively. We obtain $O(b)$ error for every $b$-local property, independently of alphabet size. Under suitable pseudorandomness bounds, the rate loss vanishes for every $b=o(n)$, compared to $b=O(\log n)$ for earlier frameworks.

item.title: Over-the-Scene Computation: Illumination-Programmed Functional Sensing of Unresolvable Populations
item.description: arXiv:2611.07732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decisions about dense populations depend on how much will cross a boundary by a deadline and when the first member arrives. Conventional radar forms a range-Doppler map, whose cells add noise and whose detections merge unresolved members. We introduce over-the-scene computation, where illumination makes the scene compute such functionals without resolving members. With random echo phases, a correlator's mean output energy sums member reflectivities weighted by a kernel set by the waveform and template. The waveform's ambiguity function is this computation's transfer function, determining computable functionals and their noise cost. One readout aggregates members over a small delay-Doppler area but along a line segment growing with duration, longest for the chirp of matching slope among constant-envelope waveforms. Members predicted to share a range lie on such a line, so a chirp's mean beat spectrum is the predicted range profile at a look-ahead horizon set by its rate. For unbiased estimation, a Cramer-Rao bound over all equal-energy waveforms favors resolving members above unit signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and grouping weaker ones into unit-SNR sets. At 0.65 members per cell, -10 dB member SNR, and one sweep, the chirp's bin sum inside the boundary comes within 16% of this bound in root-mean-square error and, with 77 times fewer samples per horizon, outperforms every unbiased estimator from a coherent processing interval of equal dwell, bandwidth, and energy. No finite set of waveform-template probes determines an unconstrained Rayleigh-fluctuating population's first arrival, but bisection localizes it if first arrivals outweigh later arrivals' sidelobes.

item.title: Quantum Communication and Phase Sensing over a Dephasing Channel with Thermal Noise
item.description: arXiv:2611.07855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dephasing is a prominent source of decoherence in quantum communication, degrading phase coherence and transmission reliability. Therefore, knowledge of the physical channel parameters for reliable transmission is imperative, motivating the integration of quantum communication and sensing at the physical layer. Consequently, we study the transmission of coherent states over a von Mises dephasing channel affected by thermal noise. We consider a heterodyne receiver, for which, we first derive the symbol-error probability (SEP) and an accurate closed-form approximation, through which an irreducible asymptotic error floor due to the dephasing channel is identified. We note that the derived SEP is affected by the mismatch between the receiver's mean phase estimation and the true mean phase, thereby formalizing the interplay between sensing accuracy and communication reliability. In addition, we derive the Fisher information (FI) for the mean phase acquisition of the channel and provide closed-form lower and upper FI bounds. Moreover, the quantum FI (QFI) of the channel is studied, and lower and upper bounds on the QFI are given, which become asymptotically tight as the photon number increases. Despite the initial complexity of the FI and the QFI, the bounds given are relatively simple and effective. In addition, by comparing the FI with the QFI, we show that heterodyne detection approaches the quantum sensing limit as the number of photons increase, while an unavoidable sensing floor exists due to dephasing. Then, using the SEP and the FI analysis, we discuss the conditions under which communication and phase estimation requirements are jointly feasible. Finally, numerical results validate the derived SEP, estimation bounds, and the sensing-communication feasibility tradeoff.

item.title: Operational Indirect Rate-Distortion Functions for Classification Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2611.07946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In goal-oriented communications, indirect source coding involves two sources: a semantic source $X$ and an observation $Z$, which is the only source available at the encoder. In this paper, we consider this framework for classification, where the decoder only needs to reconstruct $X$. We argue that the gap between the indirect rate-distortion function and the performance of practical learned coding schemes, such as variational information bottleneck (VIB) and variational autoencoder (VAE) architectures, comes from three effects: the latent representation, the choice of the deep neural network (DNN) architecture and training loss, and whether the encoder is aware of the task. To quantify these effects, we introduce four operational rate-distortion functions that account for the DNN architecture and the training loss, and we establish a hierarchy among them. We then derive these functions for a Gaussian mixture source, where $X$ is the mixture state. Numerical results, both for the Gaussian mixture and for practical coding schemes on the CIFAR-100 dataset, quantify the rate loss incurred by each effect.

item.title: Between Hi-Fi and MMI: the overlap of redundancy and synergy in partial information decomposition
item.description: arXiv:2611.08131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Partial information decomposition (PID) splits the information that two sources carry about a target into redundant, unique and synergistic parts, with nonnegative decompositions lying on a segment where redundancy measures are bounded by the positive part of the co-information and the smaller source-target information. We parameterize this segment by the overlap, the common excess of redundancy and synergy over their net balance, and show that for many of the named PID measures, their redundancy can be written as the largest positive part of the co-information over a set of reference distributions. This common form induces an ordering of those PIDs on the segment. With the smallest redundancy and synergy and the largest unique atoms of any nonnegative PID, the information-theoretic version of Hi-Fi, a feature-importance method, is the zero-overlap end of the segment for two sources, with the maximum overlap bound given by the minimum mutual information (MMI) PID. We introduce, by splitting the co-information into a pairwise maximum- entropy part and the third-order connected information, a PID that sits at zero overlap except when pairwise redundancy and triadic synergy coexist. For three or more sources the bivariate results hold on every pair of merged source groups, and among all nonnegative solutions of the lattice equations MMI and Hi-Fi still give the smallest and largest unique atoms but zero overlap on all pairs at once is often unattainable. Two inequalities across pairs are necessary in general and sufficient for three sources. For identity targets zero overlap is possible exactly when the sources' information diagram is nonnegative. In random three- and four-source distributions zero overlap on all pairs fails in 21-100% of the cases.

item.title: Drift-Resilient Predictive Interference Management: Online Adaptation of an Extreme-Value Predictor
item.description: arXiv:2611.08132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predictive interference management supports ultra-reliable low-latency communication (URLLC) by allocating finite-blocklength resources against a high conditional quantile of next-slot interference. Building on an extreme-value-theory/kernel-density-estimation (EVT/KDE) predictor with quantile-defined interference states, this paper makes the predictor resilient to unannounced shifts in the interference distribution. Its cumulative refitting on all past observations does not specify how the state partition and retained samples should evolve after a regime change. We show that drift first makes the quantile partition inefficient: cumulative refitting preserves tail support and coverage but cannot recover conditional resolution, and pays for it in channel use, whereas discarding history starves the tail estimator. We therefore propose event-triggered quantile-space adaptation. A nonparametric cumulative sum (CUSUM) on the predictor's level stream detects change. At each confirmed event, the quantile partition is re-derived from post-change observations, retained history is re-binned under it, and each state is refit from a bounded per-state memory, capped to balance stale-regime bias against tail-estimation variance, with a closed-form L-moment tail estimator. At a nominal coverage target $\eta\!=\!0.99$, relative to matched cumulative refitting with fixed states, the proposed method reduces channel use by $5.7$--$13.2\%$ and quantile pinball loss by $25$--$50\%$ across abrupt, incremental, compound, downward, and reversal drift, with coverage changing by $-0.5$ to $+1.0$ percentage points. At matched achieved coverage, it saves $4$--$18\%$ of channel uses, while resource use in load-only and stationary cases changes by less than $0.5\%$. With $K$ samples per state and $L$ states, predictor memory is bounded at $O(KL)$ rather than growing as $O(t)$.

item.title: Uniform Three-Fold Product Expansion of Algebraic-Geometry Codes over a Fixed Field
item.description: arXiv:2611.08172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A collection of classical codes $C_1,\dots,C_m$ has product expansion if every low-weight word in the sum of their extensions to the product space can be written as a sum of words supported on few lines, each line being a codeword of the corresponding $C_i$. For $m=2$ product expansion is equivalent to robust testability of the tensor code, while for $m\ge 3$ it is strictly stronger; it is the hypothesis on the local codes behind recent constructions of good quantum LDPC codes, good quantum locally testable codes, and quantum codes with transversal non-Clifford gates. No explicit family over a fixed field was previously known to achieve constant rate, linear distance for both the code and its dual, and 3-fold product expansion at growing length. We prove that for the one-point evaluation codes $C_i$ of length $N_i=728\cdot27^{\,i-1}$ and pole order $\lfloor N_i/5\rfloor$ on the Garcia--Stichtenoth tower over $\mathbb{F}_{729}$, the triple $(C_i,C_i,C_i)$ has product expansion with a constant independent of $i$. The dual codes $C_i^\perp$ then form an explicit fixed-field family of rate tending to $109/130$ and relative distance at least $8/65$. The proof is geometric: we view the words of the sum code as arrays on the product of three copies of the $i$-th curve of the tower, where the parity checks are sections of a line bundle. An exact generation theorem describes the sum-code words supported on the grid footprint of a suitable divisor. A support-localisation argument then shows that every low-weight array lies on such a divisor, after deleting a small number of coordinates. We also give a sufficient criterion for three-fold product expansion in terms of degree and genus ratios, yielding explicit families over every non-prime finite field of order at least $512$. The principal conclusions have been formally verified in Lean 4.

item.title: NOMA Assisted Coordinated Beam Hopping for VLEO Satellite Communication Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.08174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates a non-orthogonal multiple access assisted coordinated beam hopping (NOMA-CBH) scheme in multidimensional very low Earth orbit (VLEO) satellite communication systems, where multiple satellites employ CBH and coordinated beams jointly serve ground users and a dedicated ground station (GS). To characterize the VLEO-specific propagation environment, we develop a channel model that incorporates atmospheric attenuation, Doppler effects, and pointing perturbations. Building upon this architecture and channel model, a low-complexity decoupled (LCD) algorithm is designed to optimize beam scheduling and power allocation. We further derive closed-form outage probability expressions for the ground users and the GS, perform asymptotic analysis to characterize their diversity orders, and evaluate the delay-limited throughput. Simulation results demonstrate that: i) The NOMA-CBH with LCD algorithm achieves an enhanced system sum rate relative to orthogonal multiple access with coordinated beam hopping (OMA-CBH); ii) Across the considered heterogeneous traffic-demand operating points, the NOMA-CBH scheme achieves higher aggregate delivered traffic than the benchmark schemes; and iii) The outage performance of NOMA-CBH is better than that of OMA-CBH.

item.title: Common zeros of homogeneous polynomials and the weight hierarchy of projective Reed-Muller codes
item.description: arXiv:2611.08203v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We determine the maximum number of common zeros in projective space of any set of linearly independent homogeneous polynomials of the same degree, when the degree is smaller than the cardinality of the finite field. This proves the conjecture of Beelen, Datta and Ghorpade and determines the complete weight hierarchy of the corresponding projective Reed-Muller codes. The proof uses Green's hyperplane restriction bound, combined with a footprint argument that reduces the problem to the affine case solved by Heijnen and Pellikaan. Wei duality then determines the hierarchy in sufficiently large degrees, recovering the complete hierarchy in every degree for the projective plane. Finally, we prove an upper bound valid in every degree, and conjecture that it is always sharp.

item.title: Dynamics Aware Past-Future Information Bottleneck
item.description: arXiv:2611.08426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The simplification of complex dynamical systems is essential for efficient estimation and control. A principled approach to this task is through the lens of information-theoretic compression. The Past-Future Information Bottleneck (PF-IB) provides a theoretical framework for compressing linear dynamical systems. However, the standard formulation often lacks structural consistency, yielding representations that are not realizable as dynamical systems. By constraining the objective to a specific manifold of block Hankel matrices, which we prove is a Lie group, we bridge the gap between PF-IB and realization theory. Our approach ensures that the resulting compressed dynamics are realizable, thereby enabling its direct application to estimation and control. We demonstrate our approach in numerical simulations.

item.title: Low-Latency Coded Tensor--Matrix Multiplication for Distributed Signal Processing Systems
item.description: arXiv:2609.30567v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-scale signal processing systems, including aeronautical and aerospace platforms, increasingly rely on tensor operations, whose distributed execution is constrained by communication, memory, and latency bottlenecks. In this paper, we propose a tensor-aware coded computation framework for distributed mode-1 tensor--matrix multiplication that operates directly on tensor subtensors, avoiding explicit unfolding and preserving multi-dimensional structure. For a fixed partitioning configuration, the proposed tensor-PolyDot scheme achieves the same recovery threshold, communication cost, worker-side computation, and memory requirements as conventional matrix-based PolyDot schemes. However, by leveraging multivariate encoding, it replaces high-degree univariate interpolation at the fusion node with structured low-dimensional decoding. This leads to a substantial reduction in decoding complexity and latency, without affecting any other system metric. Additionally, the tensor-based approach improves memory locality and enables parallel decoding across tensor modes, making it well-suited to modern hardware architectures. Numerical results show decoding speedups proportional to the tensor partitioning factor, reaching up to an order-of-magnitude improvement in practical settings. These advantages make the proposed framework particularly relevant to latency-critical aeronautical and aerospace distributed signal processing systems.

item.title: Dithered Belief Propagation for Real-Time Quantum Memory Decoding
item.description: arXiv:2611.07144v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce dithered belief-propagation decoding for circuit-level quantum memory to mitigate the oscillations and trapping behavior that limit standard belief-propagation (BP) decoders for qLDPC codes. Our approach combines a quantum-adapted sign-flip mechanism with chained randomized prior perturbation. Evaluated under circuit-level noise on the distance-11 rotated surface code and the distance-12 bivariate-bicycle code, the proposed dithered decoder significantly outperforms BP and BP+OSD+CS-10. The proposed decoder achieves accuracy comparable to or better than state-of-the-art Relay-BP, especially at higher physical error rates, while trading a moderate increase in additions for about 98% fewer multiplications on average and eliminating node-level RNGs. These results suggest that dithering is a promising approach toward real-time decoding of quantum memories.

item.title: Design of a Speech Enhancement-Based Deep Semantic Autoencoder for Wireless Communications
item.description: arXiv:2611.07361v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech communication plays a crucial role in the Internet of Things and autonomous networks. However, traditional communication systems suffer from insufficient semantic extraction and limited noise suppression capability. To address these issues, we propose a Speech enhancement-based Deep Semantic Autoencoder (S-DSA) communication system for wireless communications. It consists of a dual-branch semantic encoder, a channel encoder, a channel decoder, and two semantic decoders, enabling joint source-channel coding for robust transmission. A key novelty lies in an adaptive semantic noise decoupling mechanism that disentangles target speech semantics from noise representations through an interaction module, thus maintaining semantic consistency under low SNR conditions. Furthermore, a joint training strategy optimizes speech reconstruction and noise estimation, while a lightweight testing strategy reduces complexity by disabling the noise-decoding path. The proposed S-DSA enables more effective separation between speech and noise, and yields higher robustness as well as better reconstruction quality. These findings highlight the potential of the proposed S-DSA as a practical solution for next-generation intelligent wireless communications.

item.title: Re-Planning Budgets under Admission Control in Grant-Free LEO Beam-Hopping Access
item.description: arXiv:2611.07592v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reordering low-Earth-orbit (LEO) beam-hopping visits can reduce grant-free update delivery even when each region receives the same service time. We derive the largest limit on inter-frame position changes that meets a prescribed delivery-rate loss tolerance when every group is visited once per frame. The guarantee concerns a protected beam's spatially averaged long-run delivery rate relative to optimized periodic service under exogenous re-planning. Fixed admission can favor irregular visits, whereas admission optimized for each revisit interval makes the per-visit reward concave under sufficient conditions on transmission success. Periodic service is then optimal at a fixed mean interval. The shortest and longest allowed intervals determine the exact worst-case loss, attained by feasible alternating visit orders that respect every group's displacement limit. The resulting budget requires no estimate of the revisit-interval distribution and extends to independent stationary renewal updates. In a collision example with 40 groups and 40 resources per slot, increasing the loss tolerance from zero to 1% raises the limit from 17 to 24 positions. With independent priorities, the latter retains over 90% of the priority-weighted waiting-cost reduction achieved by unrestricted ordering. Received-power simulations under Rayleigh fading support the predicted loss.

item.title: Joint Flexible Beamforming, Resource Allocation, and Task Buffering for Movable-Antenna Enabled MEC Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.07656v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The proliferation of computation-intensive applications, such as generative artificial intelligence and low-altitude economy services, demands mobile edge computing (MEC) systems that are both energy-efficient and adaptable to highly dynamic workloads. However, conventional MEC architectures rely on fixed-position antennas with limited spatial flexibility and rigid single-slot task execution models, which fail to accommodate bursty traffic and time-varying channels. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel MEC framework empowered by movable antennas (MAs) and task buffering. Unlike traditional approaches, our system enables continuous antenna repositioning to maximize array gains and decouples task generation from immediate execution via buffer queues, allowing for flexible multi-slot scheduling. We formulate a stochastic optimization problem to minimize long-term energy consumption by jointly optimizing receive beamforming, MA positions, and computing resources. Leveraging Lyapunov optimization, we transform the long-term problem into tractable per-slot subproblems and develop an efficient alternating optimization algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms the benchmark schemes in terms of energy consumption, while maintaining stable task queues under unpredictable traffic conditions.

item.title: The probabilistic bound for perfect hashing is sharp only for binary alphabets
item.description: arXiv:2611.08230v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the optimal asymptotic rate $R_q$ of perfect $q$-hash codes, a fundamental extremal problem in combinatorics, information theory, and computer science. Let $B_q=-\log_2(1-q!/q^q)/(q-1)$ denote the classical probabilistic lower bound. We prove that $R_q=B_q$ if and only if $q=2$, establishing an explicit strict improvement for every $q\ge3$ and settling the first assertion of a conjecture of Xing and Yuan (Combinatorica 43 (2023), 347--366). More significantly, we show that, for every $\eta>0$, $R_q\ge B_q+\exp(-(2+\eta)q)$ for all sufficiently large integers $q$. This improves the previously known increments of scale $\exp(-3q+O(\ln q))$ by an exponential factor. We also establish a structural limitation of the concatenation method. For pairwise uniform inner codes of subexponential length, the resulting rate bound exceeds $B_q$ by at most $\exp(-3q+o(q))$. Thus, exponentially long inner codes are necessary to achieve the new improvement scale within this framework. Our proofs combine Fourier analysis, high-dimensional simplex codes, additive permutation counts, and entropy bounds for hypergraph matchings. We further strengthen lower bounds from short inner codes and improve several known numerical estimates.

item.title: A class of asymptotically optimal authentication codes with secrecy
item.description: arXiv:2605.14823v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, a class of linear authentication codes with secrecy, which are equipped with simple encoding rules, is constructed. By means of a special Weil sum, the maximum success probabilities of impersonation attack (denoted by $P_I$) and of substitution attack (denoted by $P_S$) for these codes are explicitly derived. It is further proven that the codes are asymptotically optimal, in the sense that both the information theoretic bound and the combinatorial bound for authentication codes are asymptotically attained by $P_I$ and $P_S$.

item.title: Fluid Antenna-Aided Robust Secure Uplink Transmission in LEO Satellite Constellations
item.description: arXiv:2605.18099v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Secure uplink transmission in low-earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations faces significant challenges due to the time-varying spatial distributions of serving and potential eavesdropping satellites, particularly when their angular separations are small and eavesdropper channel state information (CSI) is imperfect. To address these challenges, this paper investigates fluid antenna (FA)-aided robust secure uplink transmission in LEO satellite constellations. To avoid frequent antenna reconfiguration, the FA positions are optimized over an observation interval and remain fixed throughout the interval, while transmit beamforming dynamically adapts to the time-varying satellite channels. We formulate an average worst-case secrecy rate maximization problem by jointly optimizing FA positions and time-varying beamforming under norm-bounded eavesdropper CSI uncertainties and per-slot secrecy rate constraints. Two new alternating optimization (AO) algorithms are developed to solve the resulting non-convex problem. For robust beamforming optimization, the S-procedure, semidefinite relaxation (SDR), and first-order approximation are employed to construct a tractable convex problem, followed by Gaussian randomization for rank-one recovery. For FA position optimization, we derive concave surrogate functions for successive convex approximation (SCA) and develop a differential evolution (DE)-based search strategy to reduce computational complexity. Numerical results demonstrate that both FA-aided schemes consistently outperform conventional fixed-position antenna arrays across different constellation configurations and CSI uncertainty levels. Moreover, the two algorithms exhibit different performance-complexity tradeoffs as the number of FA elements increases, with DE offering a computational advantage for larger arrays while SCA can achieve higher secrecy rates.

item.title: Perfect Codes As Exact Minimizers Of Quadratic Discrepancy In q-ary Hamming Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2608.01134v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Total quadratic ball discrepancy measures the deviation of codeword counts from uniformity over all Hamming balls. We prove that, whenever a Hamming space and cardinality admit a perfect code, the discrepancy minimizers among all subsets of that cardinality are precisely the perfect codes. This extends Barg's binary minimizing result and characterizes equality over arbitrary finite alphabets. At parameter sets that satisfy the sphere-packing condition and Lloyd's integral-root condition for correcting one or two errors, we give an explicit lower bound whose attainment is equivalent to perfect tiling: the discrepancy that a perfect code with these parameters would have. For one error, these include parameters at which the existence of a perfect code is open. For alphabets of size at least four, the discrepancy is an affine function of an energy with a strictly completely monotonic potential; for these alphabets, known universal energy bounds also give these lower bounds, and, when a perfect code exists, known universal optimality results also give the characterization of the minimizers. Over the ternary alphabet, complete monotonicity fails, and we prove the ternary bounds directly at all Hamming parameters and at the Golay parameters, the only nontrivial ternary cases.

item.title: Quantitative Tiling Stability From Quadratic Discrepancy In Hamming Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2608.25716v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quadratic ball discrepancy measures how uniformly a code meets Hamming balls over all centers and radii. Perfect codes minimize this quantity among codes of the same cardinality. We prove a quantitative refinement: at the parameters of every perfect code other than a one-word code or the full space, the discrepancy excess over the minimum is at least an explicit positive multiple of the discrepancy at the packing radius. The latter equals the tiling defect divided by the square of the code cardinality. This defect is the total squared deviation of the covering multiplicity from one. The comparison applies to all codes of that cardinality. For one-error perfect codes, the coefficient is at least one, and no larger constant holds for all such codes; explicit coefficients depending on the parameters can be much larger. The tiling defect also measures the failure of uniform ball noise to smooth a code distribution. Consequently, the same discrepancy excess gives explicit bounds on holes, overlaps, and divergence from the uniform distribution.

item.title: Product Expansion of Random Codes via Analytic Techniques
item.description: arXiv:2610.02512v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Beginning with the work of Dinur, Lin, and Vidick (FOCS, 2024), tensor codes with constant product expansion have been foundational to recent advances in quantum locally testable codes (qLTCs) based on cubical complexes. Informally, product expansion says that any low-weight parity check of the tensor code can be written as the sum of few parity checks of each component code in each dimension. Recent work of Kalachev and Panteleev (FOCS, 2025) showed that tensors of random linear codes have constant product expansion. In this work we initiate the study of random linear codes with prescribed automorphism groups. For every sufficiently large prime $k$, we construct pairs of rate $1/2$ MDS codes of length $2k$, over finite fields whose size depends on $k$, that have constant two-sided product expansion and are invariant under the simultaneous cyclic shift of two cycles of length $k$. This shift is the local action in the cube complexes of Rungtanapirom, Stix, and Vdovina (Internat. J. Algebra Comput., 2019). Along the way we give a proof of the existence of two-sided product expanding codes which, unlike the earlier result of [KP25], does not rely on explicit constructions of asymptotically optimal locally testable codes. Our proof relies on several new techniques that we view as interesting in their own right. Instead of working directly over finite fields, we work over the reals and use random Rademacher matrices for the generator matrices of the component codes. From here, we show how to relate product expansion to the operator norm of sparse restrictions of carefully chosen Gram matrices, which we bound using tools from random matrix theory. More generally, we propose a method for studying properties of random linear codes by lifting to random codes over $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$, which we anticipate will be applicable more broadly to existential problems in coding theory.

item.title: Sequential Change Point Detection for PSK Modulation Switching
item.description: arXiv:2610.14208v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Transmitters in adaptive communication systems may switch their modulation scheme at an unknown time, and a receiver must detect this switch quickly without raising frequent false alarms. Existing modulation classification methods label a finite block of received data and do not provide stopping rules with controlled false-alarm and delay performance. We study the sequential detection of a switch from one phase shift keying (PSK) scheme to another over an additive white Gaussian noise channel. We build cumulative-sum (CUSUM) and moving-sum (MOSUM) detectors from the log-likelihood ratio and its low-SNR approximation. For a switch from quadrature PSK to binary PSK, we derive the moment-generating function and probability density function of the approximate statistic. We use them to relate the CUSUM threshold to the average run length to false alarm and the worst-case detection delay. For a switch between any two PSK orders, we approximate the vector of overlapping MOSUM statistics as multivariate Gaussian and obtain bounds on both measures. Monte Carlo simulations show that our derived expressions for ARL2FA and WADD closely match the empirical results across thresholds, validating the accuracy of the proposed analytical approximations and theoretical bounds.

item.title: Principles of Quantum Communication Theory: A Modern Approach
item.description: arXiv:2011.04672v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This is a preliminary version of a book in progress on the theory of quantum communication. We adopt an information-theoretic perspective throughout and give a comprehensive account of fundamental results in quantum communication theory from the past decade (and earlier), with an emphasis on the modern one-shot-to-asymptotic approach that underlies much of today's state-of-the-art research in this field. In Part I, we cover mathematical preliminaries and provide a detailed study of quantum mechanics from an information-theoretic perspective. We also provide an extensive and thorough review of quantum entropies, and we devote an entire chapter to the study of entanglement measures. Equipped with these essential tools, in Part II we study classical communication (with and without entanglement assistance), entanglement distillation, quantum communication, secret key distillation, and private communication. In Part III, we cover the latest developments in feedback-assisted communication tasks, such as quantum and classical feedback-assisted communication, LOCC-assisted quantum communication, and secret key agreement.

item.title: A Particle-Based Multiuser Communication with a Budget Limit
item.description: arXiv:2611.07171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiuser networks can aggregate local observations through a shared receiver. In this paper, we study the particle budget required to recover the exact sum of binary inputs in a multiuser network. We show that, for the considered model, the minimum budget grows quadratically with the number of transmitters when the symbol duration and target error probability are fixed, even when the receiver observes all particle arrival times. Simultaneous on-off keying (OOK) achieves this quadratic scaling, while any slower budget growth makes the error probability approach one at a fixed symbol duration, regardless of the transmission and decoding scheme. We then examine how this particle requirement can be reduced by allowing longer symbol durations and more counting intervals. We develop a groupwise OOK counting (GOC) scheme with staggered group releases and sequential estimation of group input sums, accounting for delayed arrivals. Our bounds show that, when reception is based on interval counts, reducing the quadratic scaling requires both the symbol duration and the number of counting intervals to grow with network size. When both grow in proportion to network size, the minimum budget becomes proportional to the number of transmitters times its logarithm.

item.title: Few-Shot Beam Selection for Embodied AI via In-Context Learning and Conformal Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.07306v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) communications are essential for supporting massive multimodal sensory data exchange in Embodied Artificial Intelligence (EAI) systems. However, fast and reliable beam selection for mmWave communication remains a critical bottleneck due to the prohibitive overhead associated with conventional beam training. Although location-aided beam prediction offers a promising alternative, its performance is often limited by localization errors and the need for extensive training data. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework termed In-Context Learning driven Cross-Validation Conformal Prediction (ICL+CVCP) for beam prediction. The proposed framework utilizes the training-free adaptation capability of ICL, enabling effective operation with only a small number of demonstration samples and eliminating the need for large-scale data collection and model fine-tuning. In addition, the CVCP module constructs compact, distribution-free candidate beam sets that provably contain the optimal beam with a user-defined probability. Experimental results confirm that ICL+CVCP consistently satisfies the desired empirical coverage while significantly reducing pilot overhead and computational latency, thereby meeting the stringent reliability and efficiency requirements of EAI applications.

item.title: A Novel BVH-accelerated Dynamic Ray-Tracing Channel Model for Vehicular Communication Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.07311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate and efficient channel modeling is critical for evaluating the sixth-generation (6G) networks, while dynamic ray-tracing (DRT) remains bottlenecked by its reliance on channel coherence time. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a novel bounding volume hierarchy-accelerated DRT (BVH-DRT), which introduces a mechanism shift from a time-driven update in DRT to a spatial-driven update. The proposed channel model clusters complex scatterers using the BVH method as pre-processing to establish a geometric coherence distance guided by transceiver kinematics, so that the ray update intervals in BVH-DRT can be autonomously adjusted to reduce the complexity. Furthermore, the non-stationary channel impulse responses are generated to evaluate delay-Doppler (DD) domain waveforms, including orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) and orthogonal delay-Doppler division multiplexing (ODDM). Validations in vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) scenarios demonstrate that BVH-DRT achieves spatial-temporal consistency with measurements and commercial software while significantly enhancing computational efficiency. Additionally, bit error rate (BER) evaluation highlights the severe impact of high-dynamic channels on waveform performance. The proposed framework is important for designing reliable communications and robust sensing in 6G networks.

item.title: Sharp Minimum-Rate Guarantees for Power-Based Discrete RIS Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.07548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We characterise when desired-power optimisation guarantees the minimum user rate (MUR) in discrete reconfigurable intelligent surface systems with fixed precoding. For the weighted sum of desired powers, a bounded channel exists whose exact maximiser starves a user: no positive guarantee exists. For the minimum desired power, the retained fraction of the optimal MUR is at least a sharp constant set by the phase's power quality and residual interference. A semidefinite dual certifies it without enumerating phases.
