Syntactic parsing has been integrated into SA pipelines to address this, but conventional parsers introduce significant computational overhead. Recent work shows that reformulating dependency parsing as a Sequence Labeling (SEL) task can improve efficiency. We propose and compare two strategies for integrating syntactic knowledge into a neural sentiment analysis model under unified Multi-Task Learning (MTL). The first, Standard-MTL, jointly learns dependency parsing (via sequence labeling) and sentiment polarity classification using a shared encoder with two task-specific heads. The second, Contrastive-MTL, provides implicit syntactic guidance through a contrastive auxiliary objective and a syntax-biased attention pooling mechanism, without requiring explicit label prediction. Both rely on syntactic annotations during training and eliminate need for hand-crafted compositional rules or external parsing at inference. We evaluate eleven datasets spanning seven languages---the MARC corpus (English, Spanish, French, German) and seven datasets from SemEval-2022 Task 10 (English, Spanish, Norwegian, Basque, Catalan)---using four established SEL encodings. With the relative encoding, Contrastive-MTL outperforms a syntax-naive baseline on 10 of 11 datasets and surpasses the external rule-based pipeline (SELSP) that parses at inference on all six datasets where the latter applies, while being 1.5--9$\times$ faster at evaluation. Standard-MTL is more dataset- and encoding-dependent. These results show implicit syntactic supervision during training can match or exceed explicit parsing at inference without computational overhead.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Cultural Adaptation within Repeated Social Interactions
item.description: arXiv:2611.08334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Much of human culture is tacit and is typically learned through situated social interaction. As LLMs are deployed as interactive agents across diverse communities, assessing their cultural competence demands moving beyond existing question-answering approaches, shifting from what they know to how they adapt. In this work, we broaden the scope of cultural adaptation in NLP by investigating whether LLMs can adapt through repeated interactions via a sandbox environment. By reframing cultural adaptation as a continuous process of norm assimilation through social interaction, our work demonstrates that memory mechanisms foster longitudinal learning across repeated interactions, facilitate transfer to different social settings, and enable multilingual norm assimilation across five languages. Together, our findings lay the groundwork for continuous, interaction-driven cultural adaptation in LLMs.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: XBridge: Entity-Grounded Latent Bridge for Heterogeneous LLM Communication
item.description: arXiv:2608.11676v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Heterogeneous multi-agent LLM systems, where agents are powered by different model families, can outperform homogeneous configurations by reducing redundant reasoning patterns. Yet existing communication protocols either operate through text, discarding the sender's internal representations, or require architectural homogeneity for latent-level transfer. We identify the entity grounding problem in cross-architecture communication: cross-attention bridges that transfer continuous representations across different LLM families suffer from rare-token compression collapse, where entity identity is lost in the continuous bottleneck (bridge-only F1 ~30%). We propose XBRIDGE, a decode-free communication protocol that addresses this through two mechanisms. Lexical Anchor Mapping (LAM) maps the sender's original context tokens to the receiver's vocabulary, providing discrete entity anchors. A Latent Enrichment Bridge (LEB) lets the receiver query the sender's hidden states for contextual enrichment. The entity anchors ground the bridge's contextual signals to specific entities through the receiver's own self-attention. Across three model families (Llama, Qwen, and Mistral), seven benchmarks, and both communication directions, XBRIDGE outperforms text-based communication on all seven tasks for each model pair while achieving 11x lower latency, and in a same-architecture setting it also exceeds a KV-sharing baseline on six of seven tasks. LEB requires only 264M trainable parameters (3.8% of the receiver), is trained on a small balanced sample set, and adds negligible inference overhead.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Double Machine Learning for Panel Data: Identification, Specification, and a Bank Regulation Effect
item.description: arXiv:2611.07249v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper examines robustness and causal interpretation of panel estimates using double/debiased machine learning. The prototype treatment setup is the 2018 US banking regulation. Under common treatment timing, we characterize identification and nuisance restrictions and derive exact bank-level representations of specified "within" and "first-difference" scores. Simulations assess panel model transformation-induced specification bias and inference under weaker overlap. Empirically, estimates vary with asset-size classification and prior growth. Prior-growth adjustment reduces overlap-weighted estimates across four Machine Learners (ML); doubly robust estimates depend on the fitted propensity and concentrated weights. Both bank groups received relief, so we estimate differential exposure effects. The findings highlight specification issues and the relation between functional-form robustness and causal identification.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Neural Realized Measures: Forecast-Supervised Intraday Aggregation for Volatility Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2611.07287v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-frequency volatility forecasting typically separates measurement from prediction: intraday observations are first compressed into a daily realized measure using a fixed aggregation rule, and the resulting statistic is then passed to a forecasting model. This conventional pipeline therefore treats measure construction as forecast-agnostic preprocessing. We ask whether the aggregation stage itself can instead be learned from the downstream forecasting objective while preserving the statistical structure of established realized measures. We propose Neural Realized Measures (NRM), a primitive-preserving, forecast-supervised aggregation framework that retains the original measure-specific intraday contributions but replaces uniform aggregation with positive, mean-normalized context-dependent weights. Uniform weights exactly recover the corresponding raw realized measure (RRM), so the classical construction is nested as a special case. Because NRM remains an explicit weighted sum of established primitive contributions, it also retains direct bar-level attribution. Across SF, HAR, and MIDAS forecasting specifications, NRM is evaluated against corresponding RRM specifications under controlled comparisons. In Heston simulations, NRM reduces RMSE for both contemporaneous and next-day latent integrated variance across all evaluated primitive--regime combinations. On six cryptocurrencies using five-minute data, NRM improves QLIKE in all 54 paired out-of-sample comparisons, with mean gains of 7.23\%, 8.15\%, and 9.22\% under SF, HAR, and MIDAS, respectively. Validation-selected NRM specifications also achieve the lowest mean QLIKE across the six assets among the evaluated approaches. Ablation and SHAP analyses reveal systematic time-of-day and nonlinear local-context effects in the learned allocation.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Changepoint localization via nested exchangeability tests: from point estimates to confidence intervals
item.description: arXiv:2611.07399v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study distribution-free uncertainty quantification for a changepoint estimate in an offline setting. We observe a sequence with a single changepoint and are given an estimate of its location. The pre- and post-change segments are independent and each consists of i.i.d. (or, more generally, exchangeable) observations from arbitrary and unknown distributions. We introduce Changepoint LOcalization via Nested Exchangeability testing (CLONE), a novel method for constructing distribution-free confidence intervals around that estimate by testing exchangeability in nested windows centered at the reference estimate. Under these assumptions, CLONE provides finite-sample coverage for any black-box reference estimator. Using a geometrically shrinking radius grid, CLONE requires only $O(log n)$ permutation tests. We characterize optimal scores for the framework and provide practical recommendations that result in sharp confidence intervals. Under mild assumptions, CLONE confidence intervals have asymptotically vanishing normalized length. Simulations and experiments on image and text data support our theoretical findings.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Doubly-robust causal inference for multi-valued treatment regimes with recurrent neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.08077v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a doubly-robust method to estimate the causal effects of multi-valued treatment regimes on patient outcomes. A multi-valued treatment regime assigns personalized treatments from a set of competing options based on a patient's history. Existing methods for optimal treatment regimes are largely limited to binary or continuous treatments. We extend the longitudinal targeted minimum loss-based estimator (LTMLE) to accommodate multi-valued treatments by modeling treatment assignments with a multinomial model. We further integrate recurrent neural networks (RNNs) into the LTMLE framework as learners for the outcome, treatment, and censoring models, and compare this approach to ensemble machine learning. Simulation studies show that LTMLE with either ensemble machine learning or RNNs is approximately unbiased, with close to nominal coverage, whereas sequential g-computation with ensemble machine learning is substantially biased under a dynamic rule. A multinomial treatment model performs similarly to a series of binomial regressions with ensemble machine learning, but yields more stable inference when the treatment model is an RNN.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: ATHAAR: A Medieval Scientific Arabic Manuscript Dataset for Handwritten Text Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2611.08091v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Despite recent progress in handwritten text recognition, medieval Arabic scientific manuscripts remain an open challenge for current vision-language models (VLMs) due to cursive ligatures, variable diacritization, and more importantly the lack of training data. This paper aims to address this gap, by proposing the first annotation guidelines dedicated to the transcription of scientific Arabic manuscripts inspired by textual criticism, a well-established approach to historical text editing. We then propose, ATHAAR, a new dataset manually annotated following this guideline. Unlike previous resources in the field, ATHAAR varies both witnesses of the same text, calligraphic styles, and content to deal with texts but also numerals. Relying on state-of-the-art VLMs, we finally design a set of experiments to study models transfer across scripts, chapters, and treatises. Our findings highlight the limitations of current systems when faced with the specificities of ancient scientific texts.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: RouteAlign: Aligning Task Requirements with Model Profiles for LLM Service Selection
item.description: arXiv:2611.08162v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM service selection requires performance evidence that reflects the demands of the current task. Aggregate scores obscure differences in capability and difficulty, while semantically related examples can involve different combinations of skills. We present RouteAlign, which uses task requirements to structure both the measurement of model performance and the selection of services. Task requirements describe capability demand and difficulty, enabling alignment with corresponding model performance measurements. Historical requirements determine how outcomes contribute to global profiles and local capability estimates; incoming requirements determine how those measurements inform the current decision. A shared scorer integrates the evidence, and a generation-cost preference controls selection among eligible services. Evaluation across diverse tasks and heterogeneous LLM services shows that RouteAlign extends the empirical quality-cost frontier toward higher task quality. Comparisons with open Jev-style decision backends show consistent quality gains, with lower generation cost than their strongest tested configuration. Ablations support the contribution of local performance evidence, while catalog-update experiments demonstrate effective reuse of the fitted scorer with refreshed model measurements.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: ProQuant: Progressive Quantization-aware Training for Edge MLLMs
item.description: arXiv:2611.08216v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with impressive perception and understanding capabilities will enable a range of downstream applications. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements hinder the real-world implementation, particularly for resource-constrained edge devices. Quantization has emerged as an effective solution for deploying large models. While post-training quantization (PTQ) successfully retains the performance at moderate bit-width (e.g., W8A8), it suffers from severe performance degradation under low-bit quantization (e.g., W4A8), especially for small-scale models that are more suitable for edge deployment. In this paper, we propose ProQuant, a novel weight-activation quantization-aware training (QAT) framework tailored for low-bit MLLMs. First, to align the limited finetuning dataset distribution with the pretrained dataset distribution, we propose a self-relabeling (SRL) scheme to resample the responses of the open-source multimodal dataset. Second, we are the first to take a decoupled view of multi-modal (MM) understanding and language modeling abilities. We propose a progressive block activation (PBA) mechanism to prioritize the MM understanding recovery. We also introduce a vision-sensitive factor $\vec{\tau}$ that effectively identifies the MM-critical layers. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks, covering models with 2B-8B parameters, show that ProQuant significantly outperforms existing methods. For example, our W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct improves average accuracy by impressively 6.6% and achieves performance comparable to full precision counterparts with only approximately 1% performance drop. Code is available at https://github.com/yufeixue-ai/ProQuant/.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: "Blind Compliance": Coercive Control in AI Jailbreaking
item.description: arXiv:2611.08226v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The explosion of generative AI systems and concerns surrounding their rapidly scaling capabilities has led to an adversarial cycle between increasingly narrow content restrictions ("guardrails") and increasingly sophisticated structured prompting techniques ("jailbreaks"). Technological frameworks surrounding such jailbreaking remain largely focused on the system's output: whether harmful or disallowed content is ultimately produced for the user. However, this approach, which draws largely from classical cybersecurity, does not address the uniquely relational dimension introduced by generative AI: in many cases the user is not just accessing a technology via an exploit, but is in conversation with it as part of the exploit. Here we present an alternative lens which centers the interaction rather than the output. Drawing on interpersonal violence scholarship, we present a novel framework of coercive control categories with a particular focus on aspects which are embodied versus disembodied. We then map how these disembodied coercive control dynamics are structurally embedded in modern AI training paradigms, and how those embeddings are exploited via a particular suite of persona-based jailbreaks. In this lens, we reframe AI safety and alignment as not merely a technical security problem, but as another surface upon which we see enacted the relational dynamics of power and control.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Studying word order through iterative shuffling
item.description: arXiv:2109.04867v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As neural language models approach human performance on NLP benchmark tasks, their advances are widely seen as evidence of an increasingly complex understanding of syntax. This view rests upon a hypothesis that has not yet been empirically tested: that word order encodes meaning essential to performing these tasks. We refute this hypothesis in many cases: in the GLUE suite and in various genres of English text, the words in a sentence or phrase can rarely be permuted to form a phrase carrying substantially different information. Our surprising result relies on inference by iterative shuffling (IBIS), a novel, efficient procedure that finds the ordering of a bag of words having the highest likelihood under a fixed language model. IBIS can use any black-box model without additional training and is superior to existing word ordering algorithms. Coalescing our findings, we discuss how shuffling inference procedures such as IBIS can benefit language modeling and constrained generation.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Beyond Empathy: Integrating Diagnostic and Therapeutic Reasoning with Large Language Models for Mental Health Counseling
item.description: arXiv:2505.15715v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) hold significant potential for psychological support, capable of generating empathetic responses and simulating therapeutic conversations. However, existing LLM-based approaches often lack sufficient grounding in structured diagnostic reasoning and diverse therapeutic strategies, limiting their effectiveness in complex counseling scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose PsyLLM, the first large language model designed to incorporate diagnostic- and therapeutic-oriented reasoning for mental health counseling. To develop PsyLLM, we design a novel automated data synthesis pipeline that processes real-world mental health posts collected from Reddit, where users frequently express psychological distress and seek community support. The pipeline transforms these posts into multi-turn counseling dialogues and leverages LLMs guided by international diagnostic standards (e.g., DSM/ICD) and multiple therapeutic frameworks (e.g., CBT, ACT, psychodynamic) to generate structured, clinically informed reasoning traces. A rigorous multi-dimensional filtering mechanism further improves the quality and clinical fidelity of the synthesized dialogue data. In addition, we introduce a new benchmark and evaluation protocol, assessing counseling performance across four key dimensions. Our experiments, along with evaluations by professional counseling experts, demonstrate that PsyLLM consistently outperforms various baseline models on this benchmark. Code, data, and models are available at https://github.com/Emo-gml/PsyLLM.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: HyperGraphPro: Progress-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Structure-Guided Hypergraph RAG
item.description: arXiv:2601.17755v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-hop question answering requires retrieval agents to construct a connected evidence path across reasoning turns rather than retrieve isolated relevant evidence for a single query. However, in existing GraphRAG methods, retrieval and reinforcement learning are often optimized with mismatched signals: retrieval is driven by local semantic relevance, while outcome-level reinforcement learning assigns the reward by assessing the final answer without identifying which retrieval actions progress the reasoning path. We introduce HyperGraphPro, a progress-aware hypergraph RAG framework that focuses on evidence-path progress as the shared objective for retrieval and policy optimization. For retrieval, HyperGraphPro reranks candidate hyperedges using query-conditioned structural distinctiveness, combining entity-query relevance with a local-vs-global hypergraph incidence signal to favor entities that are informative in the current graph neighborhood. For policy optimization, HyperGraphPro augments uniform trajectory-level reward assignment with stepwise progress-aware policy optimization, which assigns step-level rewards according to the coverage of answer-guided target hyperedges. Experiments on multi-hop question answering benchmarks demonstrate that HyperGraphPro consistently improves reasoning accuracy over existing GraphRAG methods.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Projection-Free Evolution Strategies for Continuous Prompt Search
item.description: arXiv:2603.13786v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuous prompt search offers a computationally efficient alternative to conventional parameter tuning in natural language processing tasks. Nevertheless, its practical effectiveness can be significantly hindered by the black-box nature and the inherent high-dimensionality of the objective landscapes. Existing methods typically mitigate these challenges by restricting the search to a randomly projected low-dimensional subspace. However, the effectiveness and underlying motivation of the projection mechanism remain ambiguous. In this paper, we first empirically demonstrate that despite the prompt space possessing a low-dimensional structure, random projections fail to adequately capture this essential structure. Motivated by this finding, we propose a projection-free prompt search method based on evolutionary strategies. By directly optimizing in the full prompt space with an adaptation mechanism calibrated to the intrinsic dimension, our method achieves competitive search capabilities without additional computational overhead. Furthermore, to bridge the generalization gap in few-shot scenarios, we introduce a confidence-based regularization mechanism that systematically enhances the model's confidence in the target verbalizers. Experimental results on seven natural language understanding tasks from the GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our proposed approach significantly outperforms existing baselines.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Sign Language Recognition and Translation for Low-Resource Languages: Challenges and Pathways Forward
item.description: arXiv:2605.12096v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sign languages are natural, visual-gestural languages used by Deaf communities worldwide. Over 300 distinct sign languages remain severely low-resource due to limited documentation, sparse datasets, and insufficient computational tools. This systematic review synthesizes literature on sign language recognition and translation for under-resourced languages, using Azerbaijan Sign Language (AzSL) as a case study. Analysis of global initiatives extracts eight actionable lessons, including community co-design, dialectal diversity capture, and privacy-preserving pose-based representations. Turkic sign languages (Kazakh, Turkish, Azerbaijani) receive special attention, as linguistic proximity enables effective transfer learning. We propose three paradigm shifts: from architecture-centric to data-centric AI, from signer-independent to signer-adaptive systems, and from reference-based to task-specific evaluation metrics. A technical roadmap for AzSL leverages lightweight MediaPipe-based architectures, community-validated annotations, and offline-first deployment. Progress requires sustained interdisciplinary collaboration centered on Deaf communities to ensure cultural authenticity, ethical governance, and practical communication benefit.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Your Multimodal Speech Model Says I Have a Face for Radio
item.description: arXiv:2605.30472v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As large neural models have become better at language tasks, researchers are increasingly building multi- and omnimodal models that handle more than one modality of data. One example is the expansion of speech recognition models to audio-visual data, the goal being noise mitigation and multimodal subtitling. While performance and bias have been studied extensively in the single-modality regime, it is unknown how new modalities affect this, even though they produce biases in humans. We therefore propose the first bias evaluation of multimodal speech recognition, where we create videos pairing different faces with the same audio using lip-sync, and measure changes in speech transcription accuracy. We find large quality-of-service differences across mWhisper-Flamingo and Gemini models, with drops of up to 4.05 word error rate points, across self-declared gender, ethnicity, and their intersection. Our findings point to a priority for developers to evaluate, fix, and communicate such limitations, as providing more signals through additional modalities is not necessarily better, and may even lead to biased outcomes.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Influcoder: Distilling Decoders' Gradient Influence Rankings into an Encoder for Data Attribution
item.description: arXiv:2606.13668v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: With the growth of LLMs' (Large Language Models) capabilities, there has been an increasing push to curate high quality datasets by filtering samples in the training data. In general, Data Attribution (DA) methods aim to estimate how individual samples in a training dataset can precondition a model to generate certain outputs. As an example, one might be interested in which samples in the data could be the source of toxic behavior after training the LLM. Many methods quantify this conditioning through the paradigm of influence functions. While methods of this family are effective in its function, they lack the necessary processing speed and storage compactness to be practically implemented on large datasets. We propose a method, Influcoder, as a quick and cost-effective approach to influence-based Data Attribution at scale.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Soft Token Alignment for Cross-Lingual Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2606.26466v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multilingual large language models often produce inconsistent reasoning and answers for semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. Prior work suggests that intermediate representations can be relatively language-agnostic, but generation becomes increasingly language-specific as models commit to discrete output tokens. This is problematic because language-specific lexical choices can cause semantically equivalent reasoning paths to diverge across languages. These divergences motivate searching for a cross-lingual alignment signal that is less tied to any single vocabulary item or script. We propose SOLAR, an auxiliary objective for supervised fine-tuning that aligns soft-token representations across languages, using English as a pivot. Soft tokens are probability-weighted mixtures over the vocabulary embeddings, yielding continuous representations that can aggregate information from semantically related tokens across languages. We then align each non-English soft-token summary to its English counterpart in the shared embedding space. Across four multilingual reasoning benchmarks, SOLAR improves accuracy by up to +17.7 points over the base model and +3.8 over standard supervised fine-tuning, with the largest gains on low-resource languages. SOLAR also strengthens final-layer cross-lingual similarity and substantially reduces language-cluster separability, suggesting that aligning soft-token representations helps preserve shared semantic structure during multilingual reasoning.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Vision-Default, Prior-Override: Causal Mechanisms of Perception-Knowledge Conflict in Vision-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2606.28273v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-language models must reconcile visual evidence with memorized world knowledge when the two conflict. How they resolve this conflict shapes the reliability of multimodal systems, yet prior work characterizes it behaviorally without a component-level causal account. We combine activation patching across three granularities (residual stream, attention heads, and MLP sublayers) with model-component ablation studies and mechanistic analysis. Across three VLM families, we find that visual grounding emerges by default, whereas prior grounding depends on a small set of causally necessary attention heads (2.5-4.8%) concentrated in the second half of the network. These heads enable answers from stored world knowledge (e.g., "red" for a strawberry) despite conflicting visual input. Ablating them flips predictions from knowledge-grounded to visually grounded answers in 68-96% of cases under prior-knowledge prompts, but changes only 0.8-7.5% of visually grounded predictions, establishing an asymmetric causal structure. The identified heads decompose into routing heads, which modulate information flow, and writing heads, which directly project answer tokens into the residual stream. This structure is consistent across model families and scales, revealing a sparse causal circuit underlying perception-knowledge conflict in VLMs.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Parametric Skills
item.description: arXiv:2606.30015v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For LLMs, skills are textual recipes encoding mature problem-solving experience. Despite widespread deployment, their utility is limited by the model's ability to comprehend and follow skill instructions. To address this limitation, we propose ParametricSkills, a framework that parameterizes textual skills at test time, enabling context-free management of the full skill lifecycle. Specifically, we first construct a large-scale and high-quality skill collection, and then synthesize single-turn and multi-turn skill-exploitation trajectories. Using this data, we then train a hypernetwork that parameterizes both the content and the exploitation methodologies of skills by converting textual skills into LoRA adapters. To facilitate the real-world application of our framework, we further align the hypernetwork on complex, long-horizon trajectories collected with OpenCode, enabling the models to operate reliably in realistic interactive workflows with ParametricSkills. Across evaluations, ParametricSkills effectively parameterizes skills, yielding substantial gains in task completion. More notably, as parametric skills accumulate as adapters rather than crowding the context, they open a preliminary but promising path toward continual learning at test time.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: SeKV: Resolution-Adaptive KV Cache with Hierarchical Semantic Memory for Long-Context LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2606.31145v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models increasingly operate over long contexts, where the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length and dominates memory during decoding. Token eviction discards entries permanently, and semantic compression fixes each unit's resolution at prefill, so detail that becomes relevant later cannot be recovered. We propose SeKV, a resolution-adaptive KV cache built around a trained zoom-in mechanism that decides at decode time which compressed spans to restore to token resolution. SeKV segments the context at high-surprisal positions, keeps anchor tokens and span summaries on GPU, and offloads low-rank factors of each span's keys and values to CPU. Lightweight per-head routers select query-relevant spans, which are reconstructed with a learned per-span rank. The cache is lossy but non-evicting: every span stays in attention, coarse or reconstructed. The base LLM stays frozen, and the router adds under 0.1% parameters. Across five backbones and four benchmarks at a 10% GPU-resident KV budget, SeKV outperforms every method that fixes resolution at prefill, improving over the strongest semantic baseline by 2.9 points (5.5% relative). It matches exact-recall offloading caches on LongBench and InfiniteBench and trails on synthetic exact retrieval, while transferring 3 times less data per decoding step than ShadowKV and using the least total memory among the methods we profile. At 128K context, it halves peak GPU memory and cuts total memory by one third relative to full KV caching.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: TACG: Trajectory-Aware Commit Gating for Diffusion Language Model Decoding
item.description: arXiv:2607.03236v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion language models predict many masked positions at each denoising step, but their efficiency and output quality depend on which predictions enter the evolving context. Confidence is informative but incomplete for this decision: at matched confidence, proposals with different identity and support histories exhibit different one-step revision rates. We propose Trajectory-Aware Commit Gating (TACG), a training-free decoder that separates the current token proposal from the decision to commit it. TACG scores temporal support for the current proposal by contrasting its logits with an exponential moving average of earlier logits, requires the proposal identity to persist through a History Gate, and promotes a capped number of additional positions per step. The gate decides which positions to commit and when; every written token remains the contemporaneous base proposal. On complete four-task LLaDA evaluations under the stated single-seed protocol, measured task-specific operating points reach 51.02\% mean accuracy with 67.82 mean model evaluations, compared with 48.00\% and 76.59 for Native Confidence. Under a matched per-event commit-count replay, history-guided selection exceeds confidence ranking by 8.3 accuracy points at identical per-sample NFE. History-reference interventions alter commitment timing while preserving the base-proposal write rule. Experiments on Dream and LLaDA2-Mini characterize quality--cost behavior across backbones and generation lengths. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Clarence-CV/TACG-DLLM.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: The Judge is Part of the Experiment: Auditing Peer Context Sensitivity in LLM-Based Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2608.04463v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based judges are increasingly used to evaluate AI systems. An underexplored area is applying these judges to multi-agent systems, where they may see the interactions behind a final answer. These interactions, which we call peer context, can affect an evaluation in two ways: (1) they can change the answer produced by the multi-agent system, because an agent might be swayed by other agents, and (2) they can change how a judge evaluates that same answer, depending on whether the judge sees them. In this paper, we separate these two effects through a controlled experiment. We first let an agent answer a question and then answer again after seeing peer responses. We then prompt judges to rate the same final answer with and without the peer context. Finally, we check whether the judges' ratings establish a valid measure of answer quality. Across three benchmarks, four open-weight LLMs as agents, and six judges, we find that peer context changes not only the answer but also how an identical answer is judged, and judges react to it in opposite directions. Moreover, providing peer context for a wrong answer misleads agents more than correct peers help them; without the correct answer, judges struggle to tell known-correct from known-wrong answers---a problem that a well-fitted statistical model does not reveal. Our results show that even when evaluating the same answer, how a judge is set up can change the conclusions differently. We therefore call for evaluations to report what each judge sees, document detailed results per judge, and validate rating scales. These practices are an important step toward the accountable use of LLM-based judges.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Where Does Retrieval-Based Open-Ended Evaluation Fail? Automatic Taxonomy Induction from Long-Form Medical Answer Factuality Verification
item.description: arXiv:2609.30467v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Retrieval-based factuality evaluation, where LLM-generated claims are verified against evidence from authoritative medical corpora, has become the dominant paradigm for scalable hallucination detection in high-stakes clinical settings. Despite the urgency of reliable and transparent medical fact verification, most systems measure performance with aggregate metrics like F1, which obscure where and why failures occur. Existing RAG diagnostics require gold answers or annotated gold evidence, neither of which exists in this regime. We introduce two comprehensive taxonomies, grounded in a case study on the open-ended MedExpert dataset and 3 closed-ended datasets, decomposing failures into retrieval-stage errors along five quality dimensions, and verifier-reasoning errors into six consecutive steps. We adapt an automatic pattern induction pipeline using LLM-as-Judge to label evidence quality and classify verifier reasoning errors at scale, and then stress-test our findings across 4 retrieval methods and 6 frontier verifier models. Our analysis reveals that scaling model size, adding reasoning effort, expanding to authoritative web sources, and applying medical fine-tuning do not resolve these failure modes, demonstrating that they represent fundamental limitations of the retrieve-then-verify paradigm in open-ended medical settings rather than artifacts of outdated systems. We release our code and data at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Medical_RAG_eval-4AB5 for the full reproducibility of our results.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: ToolSearcher: Optimizing Tool Selection at Scale via Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2609.30906v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at natural language processing but struggle to interact with external environments. Tool learning provides a promising way to extend LLMs into actionable agents, where tool selection is a critical prerequisite for successful tool use. Existing work often assumes a small or predefined set of tools, leaving large-scale tool selection underexplored. Real-world repositories contain a vast and diverse array of tools, making it difficult for LLMs to effectively search, distinguish, and compose tools under context-length constraints. We identify large-scale tool selection as a new challenge for agentic reinforcement learning, highlighting that existing RL methods for knowledge-based question answering are inadequate for selecting tools while considering compatibility. To address this challenge, we propose ToolSearcher, a novel RL framework for effective multi-turn search and fine-grained optimization in large-scale tool selection. Specifically, we introduce category-constrained tool discrimination to improve the model's ability to distinguish functionally similar tools, event-level search modeling to explicitly optimize the discovery of target tools during multi-turn search, and trajectory-aligned credit allocation to provide fine-grained reward signals for different stages of the search-selection process. Extensive experiments on large-scale tool selection benchmarks demonstrate that ToolSearcher consistently outperforms a set of strong baselines in challenging settings involving iterative search and complex tool composition.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: P2N: Reusing Deep Representations for Greater Effective Depth
item.description: arXiv:2610.25076v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mathematical problem solving and autonomous agents are increasingly important applications of language models, demanding stronger reasoning capabilities. Computational depth is a key resource for such reasoning, but adding model layers increases both training and inference costs, while test-time scaling incurs substantial additional inference computation. We introduce P2N (Previous to Next), which reuses the previous token's deep representations, already available during generation, to increase effective computational depth with negligible decoding overhead. Specifically, P2N adds the previous token's deep hidden state to the current token's shallow representation, allowing subsequent layers to build on previously completed deep computation. This recurrence extends effective computational depth across tokens, while introducing only a single vector addition per decoding step. We train the recurrence using parallel Jacobi updates restricted to a middle-layer core. Experiments with Qwen-style models show that, at 1.5B parameters, P2N improves GSM8K accuracy by over 10 percentage points under both zero-shot and few-shot prompting, with nearly unchanged decoding latency. The benefits also extend to language modeling and average performance on general downstream benchmarks. on general downstream benchmarks.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Each Insufficient in Its Own Way: Calibrating Language Models Across Varying Evidence States
item.description: arXiv:2610.33237v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How can a language model know whether it has enough evidence to answer? Language models tend to answer even when the evidence they have is insufficient. Deciding whether to answer or gather more evidence requires a calibrated estimate of how likely an answer is to be correct with the available evidence. However, most calibration work treats the input as fixed, without asking how this estimate should change with the evidence. We introduce evidence-state calibration, which requires a model's confidence before answering to match its probability of answering correctly and to change accordingly whenever the evidence changes this probability. We propose SuffiCE (Sufficiency Confidence Estimation), which fine-tunes the confidence already present in a model's next-token distribution to match how often the model answers correctly from each evidence state. Across clinical diagnosis and multi-hop question answering with four models from two families, SuffiCE reduces the Brier score by up to 60% and increases AUROC by up to 0.16. Its confidence matches the empirical success rate and responds not only to the amount of evidence but also to which evidence is present, showing that models can learn to judge whether their current evidence is enough to answer.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Two Uncertainties Are Not One: Disagreement versus Decision-Risk in Cheap Structured Content Moderation
item.description: arXiv:2610.33258v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Content moderation compresses a graded, contested human judgment into a binary act (leave up / take down) over billions of items, at a scale where running a frontier LLM on every post is uneconomical. A new class of frozen "System One" models returns typed, calibrated decisions instead of text at ~USD 0.000025 per call and ~100 ms. We run the first independent audit of one such model on 142,658 human-labeled comments, and benchmark it against 14 frontier reasoning models (the GPT-5.x, Claude, Gemini 3, and Grok families) on a shared probe set. Two findings stand out. First, the cheap model is accuracy-competitive: its zero-shot classification AUROC (0.83) is not statistically separable (paired bootstrap, n=56; a failure to reject parity, not proof of equivalence) from 13 of the 14 frontier systems while costing 1-3 orders of magnitude less, and it is no worse calibrated than several of them. Second, "confidence" conflates two uncertainties that come apart: human disagreement (where annotators split on satire and coded language) and decision risk (where the automatic action is costly-wrong). Under an asymmetric moderation loss these call for opposite escalation signals, so no single confidence number serves both. Because the model prices extra questions at nearly zero, decomposing the judgment into parallel sub-questions and reading their spread recovers a human-disagreement signal that the model's native confidence misses -- but this remedy is specific: it helps the weakest, disagreement-blind models and only when the decomposition aligns with the sources of disagreement; a specialist toxicity model and the strongest LLMs do not need it, and the effect is distribution-sensitive. We will release the instrument, the cached runs, and the analysis.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: FindLink: Learning to Assess Scientific Connections from Source-Grounded Premises
item.description: arXiv:2611.02545v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific discovery from the literature requires assessing connections among findings obtained under different study conditions. Source attribution makes individual findings traceable, but does not determine what they jointly support. We introduce GI-TraceBench, a benchmark of 10,282 questions in gastrointestinal oncology that unifies provenance question answering, knowledge discovery, and hypothesis evaluation through shared Paper, Claim, and Evidence Span records. We further propose FindLink, a two-stage framework for provenance-grounded scientific reasoning. Premise Grounding constructs source-bound premises with explicit study context and support status. Structured Reasoning organizes these premises into support plans that represent both supported relations and unresolved conditions, then generates evidence-conditioned answers using deterministic compiler feedback. The compiler verifies structural and source-binding consistency, but does not assess scientific entailment. On the 1,545-question fixed-evidence test set, FindLink improves the balanced family macro score from 67.95 to 87.25 over direct supervised fine-tuning of the same backbone. A retrained variant without Structured Reasoning achieves slightly higher premise-identifier F1, but substantially lower relation and evidence-sufficiency F1. These results indicate that scientific reasoning requires not only identifying grounded premises, but also assessing what connections those premises support.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Beyond Maximum Likelihood: Variational Inequality Estimation for Generalized Linear Models
item.description: arXiv:2511.03087v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generalized linear models (GLMs) are fundamental tools for statistical modeling, with maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) serving as the classical approach for parameter inference. While MLE performs well for canonical GLMs, it can become computationally challenging in more general settings with non-canonical, non-smooth, or saturating link functions, where the resulting optimization landscape may be ill-conditioned, non-convex, or non-differentiable. In this paper, we study an alternative estimation framework based on variational inequalities (VIs), which formulates GLM estimation through an operator-based equilibrium condition rather than likelihood minimization. We analyze the VI estimator from a statistical perspective and establish finite-sample error bounds and asymptotic normality, together with convergence guarantees for fixed-point and stochastic approximation algorithms. The framework accommodates a broad class of link functions, including non-canonical, non-smooth, and non-monotone cases satisfying a strong Minty-type condition, and extends naturally to generalized additive models (GAMs) via basis expansion. Numerical experiments demonstrate that under a fixed iteration budget, the VI approach achieves competitive estimation accuracy and faster, more stable convergence than MLE, particularly in GLMs and GAMs with non-canonical or non-smooth link functions.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: EvoDesign: Agentic Editable Diagram Creation via Design Expertise Evolution
item.description: arXiv:2604.09568v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: High-fidelity diagram creation requires coordinated visual-spatial decisions over semantic topology, visual styling, and geometric layout. Existing methods face a representation gap: pixel-based generation offers limited object-level control, while code-based synthesis provides executable structure at the cost of intuitive manipulation. We introduce EvoDesign, an agentic framework for editable diagram creation through an intermediate canvas schema that is both machine-actionable and directly manipulable by users. EvoDesign first constructs a diagram manifest through coordinated structure, style, and layout agents, and then renders the manifest in a diagnostic verification environment. This environment produces objective defect signals and VLM-based critique, enabling localized refinement of the current diagram while also providing evidence for long-term design expertise evolution. The evolution mechanism distills refinement traces into a three-tier design expertise memory, where candidate strategies are linked to the verification evidence that supports them and are promoted into broader guidelines and principles only through repeated cross-context support. We further define CanvasBench, a canvas-recoverable benchmark and evaluation protocol with content, visual, and cognitive dimensions. Experiments across pixel, code-based, agentic, one-shot schema, and canvas-native methods show that EvoDesign provides the strongest overall balance across content fidelity, visual organization, and cognitive usability. Our code is available at https://github.com/GeminiLight/EvoDesign.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Empirical Bayes Rebiasing
item.description: arXiv:2605.08069v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study methods for simultaneous analysis of many noisy and biased estimates, each paired with an even noisier estimate of its own bias. The analyst's goal is to construct short calibrated intervals for each parameter. The standard debiasing approach, which subtracts the bias estimate from each biased estimate, inflates variance and yields long intervals. In this paper, we propose an empirical Bayes rebiasing strategy that starts from the fully debiased estimates and learns from data how much bias to reintroduce by estimating the unknown bias distribution. We provide convergence rates for the coverage of our intervals when the bias distribution is estimated using nonparametric maximum likelihood. Furthermore, we demonstrate substantial precision gains in prediction-powered inference, including pairwise LLM win-rate evaluations, as well as for inference of direct genetic effects in family-based GWAS.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: GPU-accelerated Regularized Vector Multiplicative Error Models for Positive-valued Financial Time Series
item.description: arXiv:2610.08443v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The logarithmic vector multiplicative error model (log-vMEM) provides a methodology for modeling and forecasting multivariate positive-valued time series. However, the number of autoregressive parameters increases rapidly with the system dimension and lag order, posing challenges for estimation and model selection. This paper develops a regularized estimation framework for the log-vMEM with multivariate Gamma errors by incorporating hierarchical lag structures to induce sparsity and accommodate heterogeneous lag dynamics. We consider three hierarchical lag structures: componentwise, own-other, and elementwise, in combination with group lasso, group MCP, and group SCAD, adaptive group lasso penalties. Parameter estimation is carried out through an alternating block-coordinate optimization algorithm with sequential Gauss-Seidel updates, while GPU-accelerated numerical quadrature is employed to address the computational burden of evaluating the multivariate Gamma likelihood. Simulation experiments investigate parameter recovery and lag selection under different sparsity structures. The real data analysis is carried out on the realized volatility measures for Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) which allows a comparison of the competing regularization approaches in an empirical financial setting. Together, these developments provide a computational framework for sparse multivariate volatility modeling with flexible lag structures and dependent Gamma errors.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2610.13277v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Memory-augmented assistants retrieve evidence from stored conversations and documents to answer queries. Most embedding-based retrievers compare single-vector representations of queries and memories, even when relevance depends on a small part of the content. Such local evidence can be matched to queries using the contextual token representations already computed by the same embedding models. Our method uses sparse token matching to improve retrieval without additional training. Each query token retrieves a small set of matching tokens across candidate memories. The matching scores are aggregated for each memory and combined with whole-memory similarity to rank memories. An optional low-rank query adapter can be trained with supervision while keeping the encoder and stored memory representations fixed. Our method improves retrieval across eight benchmarks and multiple model families without additional training. Query adaptation further increases the gains to 13.3 and 14.3 percentage points in average Recall@10 and NDCG@10 on Qwen3-Embedding-4B. These retrieval gains translate into higher question-answering accuracy on long-term memory benchmarks.
item.dc:source: cs.CL, cs.AI, cs.LG, stat.ML updates on arXiv.org

item.title: Reliability-Security-Efficiency Trade-Offs in Multi-UAV-Assisted MEC for URLLC
item.description: The multi-uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-assisted multi-access edge computing network (MU-MEC) is emerging in the industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) for assisting resource-limited mobile devices (MDs) in processing computation-intensive tasks. To further support mission-critical IIoT applications with strict latency and reliability demands, integrating ultra-reliable and low-latency communications (URLLC) into MU-MEC is essential. However, most existing URLLC-enabled MU-MEC studies lack a unified architecture that considers both UAV control and data links, despite the importance of UAV control for stable multi-UAV coordination. Moreover, achieving efficient computation offloading while fulfilling communication reliability and security remains a key challenge. This paper proposes a novel URLLC-based MU-MEC that balances reliability, security, and efficiency while considering both UAV control and data links. We further formulate a joint UAV placement, MD association, task reassignment, and resource allocation problem to maximize the data volume reliably and securely transmitted and simultaneously minimize system latency and energy consumption. To solve this, we propose HCNN-SAC, a hierarchical multi-agent solution that employs Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) within a three-layered training framework and incorporates convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for enhanced state representation. Finally, we evaluate the reliability, security, and efficiency performance of the proposed solution.
item.dc:source: IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing - new TOC

item.title: Energy-efficient End-to-End Communication System with Spiking Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.05550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: 2030 is expected to witness the first commercial 6G systems. However, traditional modular communication architectures cannot meet the latency, optimisation, and integration requirements demanded by various sub-millisecond, data-intensive emerging 6G applications. End-to-end (E2E) communication addresses these limitations by replacing traditional processing blocks with neural networks. Nevertheless, conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs) in E2E systems use dense computation. This results in substantial energy consumption and computational resource requirements, which may not be feasible in resource constrained devices. This paper addresses the aforementioned challenge by developing a spiking neural network (SNN) encoder that targets lower encoder inference energy while maintaining communication reliability. In particular, the SNN encoder combines sparse spike activity, sinusoidal temporal modulation, and weighted temporal aggregation to map one-hot encoded messages to distinguishable transmit signals. The model is evaluated across antenna configurations and SNN timesteps to investigate the bit error rate (BER)-energy trade-off. The simulation results show that the SNN encoder achieves comparable BER under suitable timestep selections, while reducing the average estimated encoder energy by 68.93%, 52.20%, and 35.69% for SNN timesteps 2, 3, and 4, respectively, across five antenna configurations. These findings highlight the potential of the proposed SNN encoder for energy-efficient E2E communication systems.

item.title: Optimization of Joint Beamforming in RIS-aided Multi-carrier and Multi-user MIMO Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.05796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-aided multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communication is a promising enabler for beyond-fifth-generation wireless networks. However, RIS phase shifters typically rely on a tuning element (for example a variable-length stub), which can be optimally configured for only one carrier frequency at a time. This constraint complicates RIS deployment in multi-carrier systems and often necessitates additional measures, such as using multiple RIS panels or partitioning RIS elements across carriers. In this work, we propose a novel scheme in which all RIS elements simultaneously serve multiple carriers, delivering improved performance over existing approaches. Our method leverages the multiple reflections captured by physically consistent RIS models to realize the desired phase shifts for all carriers using a single stub length setting. We further develop a joint active and passive beamforming optimization framework tailored to multi-carrier, physically consistent RIS-aided systems. Simulation results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed

item.title: StarWorld: A Cross-Layer World Model for Starlink Prediction and Streaming
item.description: arXiv:2611.05832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Starlink and other low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite broadband systems exhibit stochastic access dynamics whose effects propagate from network measurements to throughput prediction and adaptive bitrate (ABR) streaming, making reasoning over multiple plausible futures essential. Existing studies mainly characterize realized traces or individual system layers, leaving cross-layer world modeling of these evolving dynamics largely unexplored. To address this gap, we propose StarWorld, a cross-layer world model for Starlink prediction and streaming. StarWorld couples learned stochastic network dynamics with executable prediction, control, and playback processes to imagine multi-step cross-layer futures, while a calibrated Trust Gate determines whether these futures are sufficiently reliable for use. On real Starlink measurements, StarWorld achieves the lowest network-future distributional errors among the comparison methods at the principal horizons and reduces pairwise controller quality-of-experience (QoE) effect error by 76%. These results support StarWorld as a cross-layer imagination environment for studying prediction and streaming outcomes under uncertain Starlink access conditions.

item.title: Coexistence-Aware Antenna Tilt and Resource Allocation for Cellular-Connected UAV Corridors
item.description: arXiv:2611.06832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cellular-connected UAV corridors reuse terrestrial infrastructure to provide predictable aerial connectivity, but coexistence with ground users (GUEs) creates competing demands on antenna tilt and physical resource blocks (PRBs). Prior work optimizes tilt for signal quality alone and does not address joint tilt-PRB planning under corridor rate and GUE delay constraints, nor the allocation policy needed when combined resource claims exceed the PRB budget. We address both gaps by formulating a joint antenna-tilt and PRB-allocation problem that maximizes GUE sum-log-rate subject to a minimum UAV corridor rate and an $ M/G/1$-based GUE mean-delay bound. We decompose the problem into two subproblems: antenna tilts are adapted via projected gradient ascent, while PRB allocation follows a techno-economic approach. Under resource scarcity, we cast the PRB scarcity as a bankruptcy problem and apply the weighted Talmud rule to balance GUE and UAV claims. Simulation results demonstrate that relaxing the GUE delay bound consistently reduces UAV rate dissatisfaction under the proposed allocation.

item.title: Uncertainty-Aware Resource Orchestration for Agentic AI Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.05392v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems powered by large language models (LLMs) execute as autonomous multi-step pipelines that dynamically invoke tools, integrate observations into memory, and iterate until a task is resolved or a resource budget is exhausted. Unlike classical workflows with fixed graphs, the aggregate compute, bandwidth, and end-to-end latency demands of such pipelines are unknown at dispatch time: they emerge at runtime from intermediate observations and stochastic token sampling, yielding heavy-tailed, multi-modal random variables. This unpredictability forces infrastructure orchestrators into a dilemma: under-provisioning risks mid-execution throttling and deadline violations, while over-provisioning wastes scarce edge or cloud capacity. Existing schedulers require a fully known pipeline graph, while edge resource-management methods rely on parametric or stationary demand models, and neither fits the unknown, non-stationary profiles of agentic pipelines. We formalize this setting as the uncertainty-aware agentic orchestration problem, where the goal is to reserve, at dispatch time, compute and bandwidth allocations that cover actual pipeline demands, and to verify that the pipeline can meet its deadline, each with a prescribed probability. We then propose Conformal Reservation for Orchestration (CRO), an online algorithm that translates a sliding window of past execution traces into dispatch-time resource allocations with finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees via conformal prediction. Simulations over heterogeneous task mixes with multi-modal and heavy-tailed profiles show that CRO is the only evaluated method that simultaneously satisfies target probabilistic coverage across all risk levels while, among coverage-feasible methods, attaining the lowest over-reservation, roughly halving the resource waste of the Chebyshev-bound baseline.

item.title: Ray-Tracing-Based Dynamic Channel Sounding With Autoregressive Wi-Fi CSI Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.05970v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Channel sounding in Wi-Fi multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems must balance channel state information (CSI) accuracy against CSI acquisition overhead. Device mobility causes channel aging, while autoregressive CSI prediction introduces errors that accumulate over sounding intervals. However, standardized statistical channel models cannot fully capture the environment-specific channel dynamics encountered in physical artificial intelligence (AI) applications, motivating the use of Sionna-based ray tracing to evaluate CSI prediction under device mobility and evolving propagation geometry. This paper develops a dynamic sounding framework that integrates autoregressive CSI prediction with signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR)-constrained interval selection. A Transformer with rotary position embedding that converts device positions into CSI sequences predicts CSI across multiple subcarriers for beamforming updates between sounding exchanges. We formulate sounding-interval selection as a predicted average-throughput maximization problem under per-stream SINR lower-bound constraints, including CSI acquisition and processing overhead. A prediction-error perturbation analysis provides the SINR bounds, and cumulative-sum enumeration globally solves the finite single-variable problem. Actual SINR feasibility holds whenever the prediction errors satisfy the bounds. Ray-tracing experiments assess channel prediction, trajectory transfer, and autoregressive prediction errors. In single-STA Wi-Fi 7 link-level simulations, predicted-CSI beamforming improves mean goodput by 67.3%, 112.7%, and 119.1% over stale CSI for linear, circular, and cosine trajectories, respectively.

item.title: Mobility-Aware Mobile Edge Computing for Energy-Balanced Data Collection in IoT-Enabled Underwater Sensor Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.06186v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Underwater wireless sensor networks (UWSNs) face critical challenges in energy imbalance, connectivity, and data collection due to harsh environments. To address these issues, this paper focuses on the problem is how to achieve energy-balanced data collection in IoT-enabled UWSNs with a mobility-aware mobile edge computing (MEC), named MECEBDC. Unlike existing approaches, the proposed scheme jointly optimizes energy-aware clustering, cluster head selection, and AUV-assisted data collection. Furthermore, we design a novel metaheuristic-based AUV routing algorithm that incorporates realistic underwater mobility dynamics, explicitly considering gravitational pressure and buoyancy forces acting on the AUV. By leveraging the computing, storage, and mobility capabilities of MEC-enabled AUVs, the proposed approach enables efficient trajectory planning and adaptive data gathering in a stable 3D underwater environment. Extensive simulations and theoretical analysis demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces node energy consumption, improves data collection efficiency, and prolongs network lifetime compared with existing schemes, making it well suited for long-term underwater IoT applications.

item.title: Explainable Anomaly Detection in 5G Networks through Continuous Time Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.06225v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: 5G networks increasingly resemble distributed systems in their design. It then becomes crucial to move beyond traditional network-based detection methods and to explore alternative approaches. In this work, we propose a formalization of 5G network exchanges as a dynamic graph, on which we apply techniques from the field of graph-based learning to detect anomalies effectively. This representation allows for fine-grained analysis of packet-level semantic content, while simultaneously capturing sequential and topological contexts, both of which are essential for identifying sophisticated and multi-stage attacks. To assess the effectiveness of this formalism, we evaluate it with the most popular dynamic graph models, demonstrating its potential for 5G anomaly detection.

item.title: Clear Human Web: Where a Person Vouches for Every Client
item.description: arXiv:2611.06286v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The web cannot tell whether a request comes from a person or from a program. Sites have checked the network address and puzzles in its place, and both have given way: automated traffic exceeds human traffic, and puzzles are solved for pay and by agents. This paper proposes the Clear Human Web, the part of the public web that sites open only to clients a person vouches for. A person's wallet presents their person identification data (PID) to one issuer, the only party that registers as a relying party, and receives a bounded number of blind-signed tokens, proofs of personhood that carry no attribute. The browser spends one token at each site that runs the gate, and the site learns that a valid token of a trusted issuer was spent, and nothing else. No field is added to the PID, no protocol is introduced, no site registers, and the publisher of a site holds the same proof as its readers. We define the Clear Human Web through five properties and seven adversaries, and state which properties the construction satisfies against each adversary. The identities a person can hold on one site in an epoch are bounded to k. The bound holds once the wallet limits a person to one pseudonym at the issuer. In the optimum k = 1, and a zero-knowledge proof of PID possession and a pseudonym per site replace the tokens.

item.title: Spatial Path Superposition: A No-Cloning Perspective on MIMO-Inspired Spatial Diversity
item.description: arXiv:2611.06306v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatial diversity is a key mechanism in classical Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) communications, where multiple propagation alternatives provide redundant observations that improve reliability in noisy environments. A direct translation of this principle to quantum communications is forbidden by the no-cloning theorem, since an unknown quantum state cannot be copied and transmitted through independent links. In this Perspective article, we argue that spatial path superposition provides a no-cloning-compatible analogue of the spatial-diversity principle of MIMO. Rather than duplicating the transmitted quantum state, a quantum carrier is coherently delocalized over multiple communication links, so that alternative spatial evolutions are experienced in quantum superposition. In this framework, classical redundancy is replaced by spatial coherence, and the communication link itself becomes part of the quantum dynamics. Indeed, spatial coherence can enhance the fidelity of the received quantum state, providing the quantum counterpart of the classical diversity gain, and can be converted into bipartite and multipartite entanglement during propagation. This implies that, under suitable coherent path control, noisy channel evolutions can contribute constructively to entanglement generation. This Perspective identifies spatial path superposition as a quantum-native primitive for the Quantum Internet, linking no-cloning-compatible spatial diversity, fidelity enhancement, entanglement generation, and coherent path control.

item.title: When Does Risk-Controlled Throughput Forecasting Actually Control Risk? A Reproduction Study on LEO Satellite Link
item.description: arXiv:2611.06307v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Risk-budgeted throughput forecasting converts a point forecast of LEO satellite capacity into a conservative bound whose overestimation rate is held at a user-specified budget, so that admission control can act on it safely. We reproduce the state of the art, BG-CFQS, on the three Starlink traces its authors used and on an independent fourth dataset, and report four findings. First, its risk guarantee is reproducible but conditional on the calibration split: under a random split we recover every published quantity, including risk-pass on 3 of 3 datasets, but under a contiguous temporal split, which is what a deployed terminal faces, it holds on 1 of 3. Second, independent of any split, the method cannot serve a risk budget below 0.15, the low end of its candidate quantile set. On all four datasets the achieved rate is identical at budgets of 0.05, 0.10 and 0.15, overshooting by 1.4x to 3.7x at the tightest. Third, static conformal calibration cannot improve a ranking, only shift an operating point; we confirm this exactly on latency spike detection, where online calibration improves AUPRC by up to 51%. Fourth, group-conditional online recalibration splits into two mechanisms. The online part replicates: it tracks the budget within 1% from 0.05 to 0.35, where static calibration is 16 to 21% off. The group-conditional part does not: on three of four datasets, conditioning on any available covariate, including measured serving-satellite geometry, is worse than not conditioning, and our attempt to predict which datasets benefit failed. What is new here is empirical, not algorithmic: we claim the findings, not the methods.

item.title: From Network Experience to Subscriber Retention: An Explainable AI Framework for Mobile Operators
item.description: arXiv:2606.04838v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents an explainable AI-driven framework for predicting net churn among prepaid mobile subscribers. The framework formulates churn prediction as a machine learning task mapped onto an industry reference architecture. Moreover, it introduces a quantile-based feature densification transform that reconciles learning features of unequal length and granularity into a homogeneous design matrix, evaluates a label-aware truncation diagnostic that sets aside low-confidence subscribers, and generates automated English-language insights describing the impact of each feature on churn propensity. We implement and validate the framework on real production data from a globally leading telco with tens of millions of prepaid subscribers spanning approximately $800$ learning features and over $250$ TB of commercial, experience, and network data. As a diagnostic, setting aside roughly $3$% of the subscribers, selected using the true labels, lifts $F_1$ on the retained subscribers to the target. This is not an achievable operating performance on all subscribers. In our data and feature set, aggregated radio access network counters carried less predictive signal than commercial and experience indicators, despite their greater representation. The quality of experience index, which is derived from network measurements, ranked second in importance. Our results also suggest that churn risk rises as subscriber value declines, with high-value segments disproportionately exposed to gradual value leakage rather than outright attrition.

item.title: The Multipath Reliable Connection (MRC) Transport
item.description: arXiv:2606.18170v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: MRC is an open, production-grade transport designed for large-scale AI/ML training over best-effort Ethernet. It extends RoCEv2 with explicit, composable primitives for per-packet multipath and sender-based congestion control, decouples packet delivery from semantic processing, adds multiple new capabilities for accelerated packet-loss recovery and adds resilience against port and path failures. This paper presents MRC and details its core capabilities and mechanisms.

item.title: GTI-mSEMP Framework : A Proposed Framework to Simulate Malware Propagation with Inclusion of Attacker-Defender Strategy
item.description: arXiv:2606.28079v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rapid proliferation of automated, multi-vector malware threats poses a significant risk to heterogeneous, resource constrained cyber-physical networks. Conventional epidemiological models often treat security defenses as static parameters, failing to capture the strategic, asymmetric maneuvers between an attacker and a defender. To address the gap, this paper proposes a Game-Theory-Integrated Modified Multi- Wireless Sensor Epidemic Malware Propagation (GTI-mSEMP) framework. This paper analyzed and compared the operational trajectories of Susceptible (S) and Recovered (R) node populations across three different operational regimes: Balanced Matchup, Exploit Surge and Hardened Defense. Numerical simulation results capture the real-time transient dynamics of the network state variables, demonstrating how the epidemic curve shifts when either the defensive or offensive scaling vectors hold an efficiency advantage. The proposed mathematical and numerical framework provides a rigorous foundation that can be deployed in highly adversarial network environments to evaluate dynamic malware propagation and predict localized node population states.

item.title: Who Needs DRAM? We Have Fiber
item.description: arXiv:2607.08407v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rising pressure on DRAM availability and contract pricing reflects generative AI's massive high-performance memory requirements. This pressure is heavily compounded by hyperscale data center expansion, which now consumes a significant portion of global DRAM output. In this work, we propose a new architecture, Fiber Memory, which reimagines the role of optical fiber in a hyperscale data center, deploying it as an active, recirculating delay-line memory for immutable data, such as large language model weights. We present a hybrid data- and pipeline-parallel optical broadcast delay-line memory architecture that accounts for fiber's physical realities. By incorporating space-division multiplexed multi-core fibers, passive optical tap-and-amplify interfaces, co-packaged optics, and centralized in-ring 3R (re-amplify, reshape, retime) regeneration, our case study evaluation suggests that Fiber Memory can eliminate redundant weight storage across tens of thousands of AI accelerators and reduce weight-delivery power by over 75% compared to traditional HBM3e configurations.

item.title: Rate-Fidelity Control for Wide-Area Quantum Links
item.description: arXiv:2608.07163v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantum network links must distribute entanglement at high rates while satisfying application-specified fidelity demands. However, wide-area deployed fiber links suffer from polarization drift which destabilizes end-to-end fidelity and forces periodic compensation. Current deployments often use active stabilization with fixed control policies, and improvements generally stem from advances in quantum hardware. Meanwhile, software control remains relatively underexplored. Here, we formulate quantum link operation as a joint control problem over tunable rate-fidelity tradeoffs and uncontrollable link drift. From this framework, we construct a link control protocol that dynamically adapts source pump power and polarization compensation to maximize entanglement distribution rate subject to a minimum fidelity constraint.
